steps.text: If the shop's pH differs from your tank's by more than 0.5, open the bag and add a little tank water every few minutes for 15 to 20 minutes. Otherwise skip this step.

summary.expert: Float 20–30 min; mix only if pH differs by more than 0.5; net across; discard bag water; lights off. Drip acclimation for sensitive species, mindful that bag ammonia turns more toxic as CO2 escapes.
summary.guided: Match the temperature first, keep the shop's water out of your tank, and let the fish settle in the dark. It takes about half an hour.

steps.expert_note: Adults about 0.5–2% of body weight a day (the two veterinary sources differ); growing fish more; less in cool water. The 2-minute test is the working rule: no need to weigh fish.
steps.text: Feed once or twice a day. Give only what your fish eat in about 2 minutes, then remove anything left over.
steps.title: Every day

steps.text: Feed small amounts twice a day or more, and give vegetable food or wood to graze on, as the species needs. They graze all day and can't store food, so they never get a fasting day.
steps.title: Plant-eaters and grazers

steps.text: Give a meal once a day or less often. Large adults are often fed every second or third day. Remove what they don't eat.
steps.title: Large predators

steps.text: Use sinking food that reaches the bottom, so they don't depend on what the faster fish leave.
steps.title: Bottom feeders

steps.text: Feed after the lights go out. Give a small portion and remove leftovers the next morning.
steps.title: Night feeders

steps.text: Give several small meals a day, at least three, of food small enough for their mouths. Never skip a day, even when other fish are on reduced feeding.
steps.title: Fry

steps.text: Feed once a day, a small amount eaten within about a minute, and only after that day's test shows ammonia and nitrite at zero or falling. Skip a day if either is rising.
steps.title: New or cycling tank

steps.caution: If reduced feeding goes on for 14 days, check your fish's condition: long cut-backs can starve them.
steps.text: Give no food today. Then feed small meals once a day until two tests in a row read zero.
steps.title: Ammonia or nitrite above zero

steps.text: Feed once a day, at the small end of the 2-minute rule, until nitrate is back under your limit. Don't stop feeding for nitrate.
steps.title: High nitrate

steps.text: Below 8 °C, don't feed: their digestion slows right down. Between 8 °C and the bottom of their range, feed small amounts every other day.
steps.title: Cold water: goldfish

steps.text: If the tank reads below your fish's range, for example after a heater fails, fix the heater first and feed half as much until the temperature is back in range.
steps.title: Cold water: tropical fish

steps.text: Healthy adult fish may go without food one day a week, if you choose. Never for fry, plant-eaters and grazers, sick fish or fish in quarantine.
steps.title: Optional fasting day

steps.text: With this many fish, feed carefully: only what is eaten in about 2 minutes, and remove leftovers. Your test results show if it's too much.
steps.title: Many fish

summary.expert: Default: 1–2 meals a day, eaten within ~2 min, leftovers removed; adults about 0.5–2% of body weight a day (vets differ). Adjust by diet group, life stage, tank stage, readings and temperature.
summary.guided: Feed once or twice a day, only what your fish eat in about 2 minutes, and take out what's left. Some fish, tanks and test results need something different; the steps below show which apply to your tank.

steps.caution: Use only fertilisers made for aquariums.
steps.expert_note: Plain gravel or sand holds few nutrients, so root feeders on it need root fertiliser. A nutrient layer of about 1 cm under the gravel, or an aqua soil, supplies the roots at first. Micronutrient-only liquids suit most planted tanks; complete liquids with nitrogen and phosphorus suit heavily planted ones.
steps.text: Plants tied to wood or rock, mosses and floating plants feed from the water, so liquid fertiliser helps them. Carpets, swords, crypts and other root feeders gain most from root tablets. Stem plants respond to either.
steps.title: Match the fertiliser to your plants

steps.caution: New aqua soil can release ammonia for weeks after it is laid. Test ammonia and nitrite, and add fish or shrimp only when your tests say the tank is ready.
steps.expert_note: One soil maker suggests 25–50% water changes at least twice a week for the first 4 weeks. In the app your test readings set the interval, with no more than 50% at once once animals are in. Ammonia becomes more toxic above pH 7.
steps.text: Nursery-grown plants carry enough reserves to root, so add little or no fertiliser for the first 3–4 weeks. Plants grown in laboratory cups carry less, so give them small amounts within a couple of days.
steps.title: Wait after planting

steps.expert_note: Estimative index (EI), for CO2-injected tanks only: dose nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and trace elements so nothing runs short, with a large weekly water change limiting build-up; targets nitrate 5–30, phosphate 1–3, potassium 10–30 and iron 0.2–0.5 mg/L, and nitrate can reach about twice the weekly dose. The app's nitrate alerts override any EI target. Lean dosing puts far less in the water because a rich soil supplies much of the rest; its only source is a fertiliser maker, and no originator's publication was found.
steps.text: Begin with less than the dose on the label and raise it gradually as the plants respond. Don't go above the label dose.
steps.title: Start below the label dose

steps.text: Follow the product's directions. Press tablets 3–4 cm into the gravel near the roots, add more under large root feeders, and watch for pale new growth as a sign they need more.
steps.title: Add root tablets where roots are

steps.text: Plants without injected CO2 use less, so dose lightly and raise slowly. Algae follows an imbalance between light, CO2 and nutrients, not one nutrient on its own.
steps.title: Without injected CO2, fertilise lightly

steps.text: Test nitrate before adding a fertiliser that contains nitrogen. If it reads above 20 mg/L, skip that fertiliser until it falls; micronutrient-only products and root tablets can carry on. Fertiliser never sets your water changes: your care plan and readings do.
steps.title: Let your nitrate tests decide

steps.expert_note: Hobby guide from one fertiliser retailer: nitrogen, potassium, phosphate and magnesium shortages tend to show first on older leaves (yellowing from the tips, pinholes, soft brown patches, pale leaves with dark veins); iron and calcium on new growth (pale new leaves with darker veins, twisted or stunted tips). Land-plant extension guides support only the old-leaf and new-leaf logic, and warn that symptoms of different nutrients overlap.
steps.text: Check the likely causes in order: light, CO2, recent planting (new plants often shed their nursery leaves), then nutrients. Change one thing at a time and wait two to three weeks before judging. A leaf photo alone can't tell you which nutrient is short.
steps.title: If leaves turn pale or damaged

summary.expert: Liquid for water-column feeders, root tablets for root feeders, either for stem plants. Nursery-grown plants: little or none for 3–4 weeks; laboratory-grown cups: small amounts within days. Start below the label dose and raise by response, never above it. Without injected CO2, dose lightly. Nitrate readings override any dosing target.
summary.guided: Match the fertiliser to your plants. Nursery-grown plants need little or none for the first few weeks; plants from laboratory cups need a little within a couple of days. Then start below the dose on the label and raise it slowly while you watch the plants. Your nitrate readings override any dosing.

steps.text: Fill with conditioned water, and run the filter and heater full time.
steps.title: Set up and run the tank

steps.caution: Use ammonia with no surfactants or scents: it should not foam when shaken. Don't overdose; far too much ammonia stalls the cycle for a long time.
steps.expert_note: Vets give 1–5 mg/L; about 2 ppm stays below levels that may slow nitrite-eating bacteria in hard, alkaline water.
steps.text: Add ammonia until the test reads about 2 ppm.
steps.title: Add an ammonia source

steps.text: Log ammonia, nitrite and nitrate. Ammonia falls first, then nitrite appears and later falls as nitrate rises.
steps.title: Test every day or two

steps.text: When ammonia drops to 0, add enough to bring it back to about 2 ppm.
steps.title: Keep feeding the bacteria

steps.expert_note: Nitrification uses up carbonate hardness; low KH lets pH fall, and the bacteria slow below about pH 6.5.
steps.text: Test pH and KH. If pH is below 6.5 or KH below 3 dKH, the bacteria slow down: do a partial water change, or add a KH buffer, then carry on dosing.
steps.title: If the cycle stalls

steps.caution: Seeded media can carry disease and pests, so only take it from a tank you know is healthy.
steps.expert_note: Bottled bacteria products are optional and unreliable; the test result, not the product, decides when fish can go in.
steps.text: A handful of filter media from an established, disease-free tank with similar water is the most reliable shortcut.
steps.title: Speed it up (optional)

steps.text: The tank is cycled when 2 ppm of ammonia drops to 0 ammonia and 0 nitrite within 24 hours, with nitrate showing.
steps.title: Check that it's finished

steps.text: Stop dosing ammonia the day before, do a large water change to lower nitrate, check ammonia and nitrite read 0, then add a few fish at a time.
steps.title: Prepare for fish

summary.expert: Dose ammonia to about 2 ppm (vet range 1–5 mg/L; the low end avoids stalling in hard, alkaline water). Cycled when 2 ppm falls to 0 ammonia and 0 nitrite within 24 h with nitrate showing. Usually 4–8 weeks. Keep pH at 6.5 or above and KH at 3 dKH or above. Bottled bacteria are optional and unreliable.
summary.guided: Grow the helpful bacteria that make fish waste safe before any fish go in. It usually takes 4 to 8 weeks, faster with filter media from a healthy established tank. Your test results, not the calendar, tell you when it's done.

steps.caution: Some bunched plants are treated with insecticides that kill shrimp, and rinsing is not proven to remove them.
steps.text: If the tank has shrimp or snails, choose laboratory-grown plants (sold in closed cups) where you can. Otherwise keep new plants in a separate container for at least a few days and rinse them well before adding them.
steps.title: Check the plants first in a shrimp or snail tank

steps.text: Take off the weight, ring or wool holding the bunch together, and strip the lowest leaves from each stem.
steps.title: Prepare the stems

steps.expert_note: In a new or emptied tank, plant with only a few centimetres of water in it, refill slowly over a saucer, and mist the plants so they never dry out.
steps.text: Push each stem into the substrate on its own, so the stems stand together as a group rather than as one bundle.
steps.title: Plant one stem at a time

steps.text: Many stem plants are grown above water at the nursery. Those leaves often fall after planting and underwater leaves replace them within a few weeks: the plant is changing form, not dying.
steps.title: Expect some leaves to drop

steps.text: When stems get long, cut the longest ones just above a leaf and plant the cut tops back in the group. The stumps branch, so the group gets bushier.
steps.title: Trim and replant the tops

steps.text: Small, frequent trims are better than one big cut, which can upset the tank's balance.
steps.title: Trim little and often

steps.text: Never put plants, plant pieces or water that contains them into ponds, rivers or other waterways.
steps.title: Never release trimmings

summary.expert: Remove the weight or ring and the lowest leaves; plant stems singly in a group. Trim the longest shoots above a leaf and replant the tips; cut stems branch. Trim little and often. Emersed-grown leaves drop and are replaced within weeks.
summary.guided: Stem plants such as water wisteria, ludwigia and anacharis go in one stem at a time, in a group. When they grow tall, cut off the tops and replant them, and the group gets bushier.

steps.text: About 60 litres or more, and wide rather than tall. Bigger tanks stay steadier and give you more choice of fish.
steps.title: Choose the tank

steps.caution: Never use soap or detergent on anything that goes in the tank. For lime scale on a used tank, use vinegar, then rinse.
steps.text: Rinse the tank, gravel and decorations with plain water.
steps.title: Rinse with plain water

steps.text: Fill slowly over a plate so the substrate stays put. Use cold tap water and a conditioner that treats chloramine, dosed for the volume as the label says.

steps.text: Switch on the filter and heater and let the tank run for a day or two, so the temperature settles and any leaks or faults show.

steps.text: Test the tap water once for ammonia, nitrate, pH, KH and GH, or get your water supplier's report. It helps you choose fish that suit your water.
steps.title: Test your tap water

steps.caution: Don't buy 'starter fish' to cycle the tank: ammonia and nitrite in a new tank poison them.

steps.text: When the cycle is done, add one group of one species, then wait and test before adding more.

summary.guided: Choose a tank of about 60 litres or more, rinse it with plain water, fill it with treated tap water, let it run, then cycle it without fish before the first fish go in. Expect 4 to 8 weeks before the first fish.

steps.expert_note: Plants rated co2 'high' need about 15–30 mg/L together with strong light and fertiliser; 'low' means about 3–15 mg/L helps but is optional. Without injection a tank sits near 2–3 mg/L, more by morning from fish and decay.
steps.text: Only plants marked as needing injected CO2 need a CO2 system. Easy plants grow without it, and plants marked 'CO2 helps' grow without it too, just more slowly. Liquid carbon products are not a suggested substitute.
steps.title: Check that your plants need it

steps.caution: Don't touch frost on a cylinder in use: it can freeze skin. If you hear a leak or feel unwell near the cylinder, close the cylinder valve if you can do so at once, open windows and leave the room.
steps.expert_note: CO2 is heavier than air and collects in low places. Ordinary air check valves can turn brittle in CO2; fit a CO2 check valve pointing with the gas flow, to stop tank water being drawn back into the regulator. A brief hiss when the regulator is fitted or opened is normal.
steps.text: Keep the cylinder upright and strapped so it can't fall, away from heat and direct sun, and not in a basement. Use a regulator made for CO2 and for that cylinder, and fit a check valve made for CO2 in the line. Brush soapy water over new connections: bubbles mean a leak.
steps.title: Set up the cylinder safely

steps.expert_note: In the dark, plants use oxygen and release CO2, and oxygen is lowest just before dawn, so the night is when fish are most at risk. A light period over 10 hours is an algae risk.
steps.text: Switch the CO2 on up to about an hour before the lights come on, and off just before the lights go out. Never run it through the night.
steps.title: Set the timer

steps.expert_note: With 4 dKH solution, green is about 25–35 mg/L (lime green about 30). A 2 dKH solution turns green at about 15 mg/L, for low-energy tanks. It shows an average over roughly the last three hours. The pH-and-KH estimate, CO2 ≈ 3 × KH × 10^(7 − pH), reads too high where aqua soil, peat, wood, phosphate or other acids are present, and a pH misread by 0.2 can turn 30 mg/L into about 45: treat it as a rough guide, never a measurement.
steps.text: Fill the drop checker with 4 dKH reference solution, never with tank water. Blue means low, green means on target and yellow means too much. Read it a few hours after any change, and aim for a darker green rather than yellow-green.
steps.title: Check it with a drop checker

steps.caution: Keepers who chase the drop-checker colour can add too much gas, because it reacts hours late.
steps.text: Start with a low gas flow and raise it in small steps over several days, checking the drop checker and your fish after each change. Don't raise it while the drop checker is yellow or after your fish have been gasping.
steps.title: Start low and raise slowly

steps.text: Keep a ripple on the water surface, day and night. Fish cope with CO2 far worse when oxygen is low, and high CO2 and low oxygen tend to come together.
steps.title: Keep the surface moving

steps.caution: Gasping with CO2 on is urgent: switch it off first. In an emergency a large water change with dechlorinated water at the same temperature works better than aeration alone, but change no more than 50% at once.
steps.text: Too much CO2 shows first as sluggish fish, then fish that stop eating, then fish gasping at the surface. If you see these, turn the CO2 off and aerate strongly.
steps.title: Know the signs of too much

steps.text: Some regulators release a burst of gas when the cylinder is nearly empty, so replace it before it runs low.
steps.title: Change the cylinder before it runs out

summary.expert: Injected CO2 for plants is usually aimed at 15–30 mg/L; 30 mg/L is the upper target in hobby sources and the app never suggests more. Merck gives below 12 mg/L as normal for fish systems and lists above 40 mg/L in its hazard table. CO2 on up to about 1 h before lights-on, off just before lights-off; keep the surface moving. Check with a 4 dKH drop checker (2 dKH for low-energy tanks), which lags by hours.
summary.guided: Only plants marked as needing injected CO2 need a CO2 system; easy plants grow without one. If you do use CO2, set the cylinder up safely, switch the gas off before the lights go out, check it with a drop checker, and watch your fish more closely than the colour.

care_guides.title: Use injected CO2 safely

sizing_rules.basis: Default while the tank profile has no room temperature; it covers a room 5 to 10 °C colder than the tank. By the gap between room and tank: up to 5 °C, 0.75–1.0 W/L; 5 to 10 °C, 1.0–1.5 W/L; 10 to 15 °C, 1.5–2.0 W/L; more than 15 °C, insulate or heat the room. Use the upper end for tanks under about 50 L or without a lid. Manufacturer and hobby rules of thumb; no veterinary or scientific source gives a figure.

summary.expert: 1.0–1.5 W/L default (room 5–10 °C below the tank). By room-to-tank gap: ≤5 °C 0.75–1.0; 5–10 °C 1.0–1.5; 10–15 °C 1.5–2.0; >15 °C insulate or heat the room. Upper end under ~50 L or without a lid. Most single heaters stop at 300 W, so tanks over ~300 L usually need two (a 284 L discus tank needs ~284–426 W); split the wattage in large or very warm tanks; two smaller heaters also limit overheating if one sticks on. 30 min in the water before switching on and after unplugging. Unplug before water changes that expose it. A separate thermometer is the failure check; external controllers aren't recommended, and some manuals forbid them.
summary.guided: Keeps tropical fish at a steady temperature. Choose about 1 to 1.5 watts for each litre in a normal room, more if the room is cold, and split the wattage across two heaters in large or very warm tanks. Place it near the filter outflow, not touching the gravel, and wait 30 minutes after placing it before switching on. Next step: put a separate thermometer at the other end of the tank and glance at it every day.

summary.expert: Timer, fixed daily period. New planted tank: 6 h/day for 2–3 weeks, then 6–8 h; >10 h flagged as an algae risk. Fish-only tanks: no source gives hours; only a day–night cycle and never 24 h. Plant light bands, approximate PAR at the plant: low 15–30, medium 30–50, high >50 µmol/m²/s; a plant's band is what it needs to grow well, not just survive. PAR falls with depth and toward the corners, and substrate colour changes it; no PAR meter needed. Watts per litre measure power use, not plant light, and don't convert to PAR or apply to LEDs.
summary.guided: Fish need a day and a night: never leave the light on around the clock, and keep the tank out of direct sun, which feeds algae and warms the water. Many fish prefer soft light with plants or cover to hide in, and sudden changes from dark to bright are best avoided. Next step: put the light on a timer and check that it works. In a new planted tank, give 6 hours a day for the first 2 to 3 weeks, then 6 to 8 hours; more than 10 hours often brings algae.

maintenance.note: Clean it when the flow has dropped or the water is cloudy; many canisters go 3 to 6 months between cleans. Unplug it before opening. Rinse the media in removed tank water, never under the tap, clean only about half of the biological media each time, and clean the impeller while it is open. Rinse the housing with water only, no soap. Don't clean it on the day of a big water change or in the week before a holiday.

sizing_rules.basis: Rated flow divided by tank volume. The upper end is for heavily stocked tanks. A hobby rule of thumb: no veterinary or scientific source gives a number. Judge the filter by readings (ammonia and nitrite at zero, clear water).

summary.expert: 4–10× turnover per hour (rated; hobby rule of thumb, no scientific source); judge it by ammonia and nitrite at 0 and clear water. What it does depends on the media loaded, and media can be stacked. Check flow every 28 days; clean when flow drops or the water clouds (retailer: typically every 3–6 months). Unplug before opening; half the biological media per clean; impeller while open; no soap. Tap rinsing is debated and risky in new tanks and with chloramine. Carbon is optional, replaced as its label says, and must come out during medication.
summary.guided: A sealed box that sits below the tank and pumps water through layers of filter media. It suits heavily stocked tanks. Pick one rated for about 4 to 10 times your tank volume per hour. You can't see the media, so check it every 4 weeks: if the flow has slowed or the water looks cloudy, unplug it and clean it in old tank water, never under the tap.

maintenance.note: Rinse when the flow drops noticeably, and at least every 4 weeks. Never under the tap, and not on the same day as a big water change.

sizing_rules.basis: Rated flow divided by tank volume, for gentle-flow fish and fry tanks. A hobby rule of thumb: no veterinary or scientific source gives a number. Judge the filter by readings (ammonia and nitrite at zero, clear water).

summary.expert: 2–4× turnover per hour for gentle-flow fish and fry tanks (hobby rule of thumb). Foam does mechanical and biological filtration; no chemical stage. Needs an air pump; an airstone inside gives finer, quieter bubbles; check valve when the pump is below the rim. Vet sources list foam filters for treatment and quarantine tanks. Rinse in removed tank water when flow drops, and at least every 28 days; tap rinsing is debated and risky in new tanks and with chloramine, and over-washing can cause a nitrite spike. Rinse, don't replace, until the foam fails (often 12–18 months), then replace a third or half at a time, at least 4 weeks apart.
summary.guided: A block of foam that an air pump draws water through. It traps dirt and holds the bacteria that keep the water safe, and its gentle flow suits fish that like still water, fry and quarantine tanks. Next step: put an airstone inside it to make it quieter, and fit a check valve in the airline if the pump sits below the top of the tank. When the flow slows, and at least every 4 weeks, squeeze it in old tank water, never under the tap.

answer.expert: Bowls and small 'fun' tanks are unsuitable (RSPCA; PetMD, vet-written). Goldfish produce heavy waste and small volumes foul fast; bowls may need up to 50% of their water changed weekly (Merck owner edition). Lifespan 10–15 years, up to 20; they grow far beyond shop size. answer.guided: No. Goldfish grow large, live for many years and make a lot of waste, and a bowl's water fouls too quickly to keep them healthy. A fancy goldfish needs at least 100 litres and an 80 cm tank for one adult, plus about 50 litres for each extra fish. A common, comet or shubunkin goldfish grows to about 30 cm and needs at least 120 cm and about 190 litres, or a pond. Either way, use a filter and keep the surface moving. If your goldfish is already in a bowl, move it to a larger, filtered tank as soon as you can; until then, test for ammonia and nitrite and follow your care plan, which tells you what to do when a reading is high.

answer.expert: feeds_from means where fertiliser helps most: water_column (epiphytes, mosses, floaters), roots (swords, crypts, bulb plants, most carpets), both (stem plants and other rooted plants that respond to either). Inert gravel holds few nutrients, so rooted plants on it need root fertiliser. New tank: little or none for 3–4 weeks, since nursery-grown plants carry reserves; laboratory-grown cups carry less and need small doses within days. Liquid: start below the label dose and raise by response. Root tabs: no fixed interval; follow the product, add more under large root feeders, watch for pale new growth. Algae follows an imbalance of light, CO2 and nutrients; without injected CO2, dose lightly and raise slowly, and never blame one nutrient. Estimative-index dosing is for CO2-injected tanks only and relies on large water changes; the app's nitrate alerts override any dosing target. Liquid carbon products are not recommended: Vallisneria and anacharis-type plants can melt with them.
answer.guided: It depends on the plant. Plants tied to wood or rock, mosses and floating plants feed from the water, so liquid fertiliser is what helps them. Swords, crypts, bulb plants and most carpeting plants benefit most from root fertiliser: in plain gravel or sand, root tablets pushed in under them help most. Stem plants and other rooted plants respond to either. In a new tank, add little or no fertiliser for the first 3–4 weeks. After that, start below the dose on the label and raise it slowly while you watch how the plants respond. For root tablets, follow the product's directions, add more under large root feeders, and watch for pale new growth. Algae comes from light, CO2 and nutrients being out of balance, not from one nutrient, so in a tank without added CO2, fertilise lightly. Fertiliser does not set your water changes: your care plan and test results do.

answer.expert:
Guideline 1.5–2 L per cm of adult tropical fish, SL (welfare charity; goldfish 4 L/cm and at least 60 L each); a magazine's 2.5 cm per 4.55 L is about 1.8 L/cm. The app reads ≥ 2 L/cm as within the guideline, 1.5–2 as near its top, < 1.5 as over it; a guideline, never 'safe'.
- Length rules fail for large fish (mass grows faster than length); a retailer limits the rule to fish of about 2.5–7.5 cm.
- Species minimum tank sizes apply on top.
- Surface area (veterinary manual): 1 cm of fish per 36 cm² of surface, less in cold water; needs tank width.
- Real limits: biofiltration, flow, oxygen, food and territory.
- Add one species at a time, with no cap on fish per addition (a cap would split shoals); only at 0 NH3/0 NO2; daily tests after each addition. While cycling, light stocking for the 4–6 weeks the biofilter needs. Readings override the index.
answer.guided:
There is no exact number, only a guideline. For tropical fish a common one is 1.5 to 2 litres of water for every centimetre of fish, measured at adult size without the tail. Goldfish need about twice that, 4 litres per centimetre and at least 60 litres each. Plan for the size your fish will reach, not their size in the shop.
- The rule works best for small fish. For fish over about 7.5 cm it is less reliable, and each species still needs its own minimum tank size.
- Your filter, feeding and the fishes' behaviour matter as much as the numbers.
- Add one species at a time, the whole group together, and only when ammonia and nitrite both read 0. After adding fish, test every day until the readings stay at 0.
- If the tank is still cycling, stock lightly and test every day.
- Your test results decide: if nitrate climbs fast, the tank has as many fish as it can manage for now.

answer.expert:
Readings set the schedule; cap any single change at 50% with livestock present.
- Fish-in cycle: partial change (≤ 50%) whenever NH3 > 0.1 ppm or NO2 > 0, daily if needed.
- Fishless cycle: no changes except to bring down an off-scale ammonia overdose or to restore KH if the cycle stalls; ~50% before stocking.
- Newly cycled (first 90 days): 25% q7d.
- Established: start 25% q14d; q7d if < 1.5 L per cm of fish or < 40 L; q21d if ≥ 2 L/cm and planted. Once the NO3 rise rate r is known (two readings ≥ 3 d apart, no change between), use the smallest f (20–50%) at q14d, else q7d, with tap + rT/f ≤ tap + 20 and ≤ 40; if 50% q7d isn't enough, reduce feeding or load.
- Floor: ≥ 20% q28d even with perfect readings (minerals, KH, dissolved organics).
- CO2-injected tanks: same NO3-led plan; no sourced high-tech routine exists.
- Overrides: any measurable NH3 or NO2 in an established tank: act today, up to 50%. NO3 > 40 ppm: act today, aiming below 20. Long-neglected tank (pH < 6 or KH ≤ 1 with NH3/NO2 > 0): 10–15% daily in week 1, every other day in week 2, 20–25% twice a week in weeks 3–4; never one large change. Tap and tank pH > 0.5 apart: steps of ≤ 15% on consecutive days.
answer.guided:
It depends on your tank, so let your test results guide you. Never change more than half the water at once while fish are in the tank.
- Cycling with fish: change some water, up to half, whenever ammonia is above 0.1 ppm or nitrite reads anything above 0. At first that can mean daily; space changes out as readings stay at 0.
- Cycling without fish: no routine changes until the cycle finishes (only to bring down an ammonia overdose or to restore KH if the cycle stalls), then change about half the water before adding fish.
- First 3 months after cycling: about 25% once a week.
- Settled tank: start at 25% every two weeks. A crowded tank, or one under 40 litres, starts at every week; a lightly stocked, planted tank at every three weeks.
- Then let nitrate decide: two nitrate tests at least 3 days apart, with no change between them, show how fast it rises, and the change should keep it within 20 ppm of your tap water and under 40. The app works this out in its care plan.
- Even with perfect readings, change at least 20% every 4 weeks: it replaces minerals and removes waste that test kits don't measure.
If your tap water's pH is more than 0.5 away from the tank's, split each change into smaller steps on following days.

summary.expert: Carassius auratus, single-tailed forms. About 30 cm (SPCA NZ, which suggests a pond); FishBase gives 48 cm TL as a record size, 10 cm as a common length. 120 cm (four times adult length, the RSPCA Australia and SPCA NZ rule) / 189 L for one fish; RSPCA asks at least 60 L per goldfish. 10–24 °C, no heater normally needed; ideal around room temperature, avoid heating above 24 °C, and keep changes within about 1 °C a day. pH 6.5–8.4 (6.5–7.5 ideal), 8–18 dGH, KH 5–15 (OATA's fancy-goldfish figures; FishBase 5–19 dGH). Strong aeration and filter turnover of at least 5× the tank volume per hour. Adults: one sinking-pellet feed a day; surface feeding is linked to buoyancy problems. High bioload. Lifespan 10–15 years, up to 20. Introduced around the world with reported harm to native wildlife. Never release fish or fry into ponds or rivers; rehome them instead.
summary.guided: The single-tailed goldfish (common, comet, shubunkin) grows to about 30 cm, can live 10 to 15 years or more and makes a lot of waste, so it outgrows most aquariums. The tank must suit the adult fish, not the one in the shop: at least 120 cm long and about 190 litres for one fish, with a strong filter and plenty of surface movement. It is a coldwater fish that normally needs no heater; keep it around room temperature and never heat it above 24 °C. Feed sinking food rather than floating flakes, and expect it to dig up and eat many plants. It can live alone but does better with another goldfish if there is room. Never release fish or fry into ponds or rivers; rehome them instead.

tank_mates.caution: Fancy goldfish, which are slower, lose out at feeding and may have their fins nipped; small fish such as white cloud mountain minnows, which adult goldfish may eat; tropical fish, which need warmer water

summary.expert: 24–28 °C (FishBase 23–26, retailer 24–26), pH 7.7–8.6, 5–25 dGH, KH 7–15. Lake Malawi measures pH 8.5–8.6, about 3.4–4.8 dGH and 6.6–7.2 dKH. 10 cm (FishBase 8.1 cm SL, retailer 12.5 cm). 120 cm / 154 L. One male to 3+ females; larger groups with more females than males, in a large tank with plenty of rockwork in mixed mbuna tanks. Mostly vegetable food, no red meat. summary.guided: One of the milder Lake Malawi rock cichlids, bright yellow and nearly always tank-bred. It needs hard, alkaline water and plenty of rockwork with caves. Feed mostly plant-based food. The female carries the eggs and fry in her mouth for three to four weeks without eating. Swelling, wasting or deaths have several possible causes, including parasites, and need an aquatic vet's diagnosis. Never release fish or fry; rehome them through a shop or club.

summary.guided: A shy night-time fish for experienced keepers, often sold wrongly as a beginner's oddity. summary.expert: Carassius auratus, fancy breeds; breed-level care has no source. 20 cm, body without fins (OATA; Practical Fishkeeping for telescopes). 80 cm (four times adult length, the RSPCA Australia and SPCA NZ rule) / 100 L for one adult, plus 50 L per further adult (OATA; SPCA NZ 75 L + 40 L; PetMD 76 L per fish); about 120 × 60 cm for three. 10–24 °C (RSPCA, PetMD), ideal around room temperature, avoid heating above 24 °C, no more than about 1 °C change in a day (PetMD care sheet); pH 6.5–8.4 (6.5–7.5 ideal; vet and welfare care sheets; OATA 6.5–8.5); 8–18 dGH and KH 5–15 (OATA; FishBase 5–19 dGH). Long or doubled fins: named among the fish most prone to fin damage and fin rot. Sinking food; surface feeding is linked to buoyancy problems. High bioload. Never release fish or fry into ponds or rivers; rehome them instead.
summary.guided: Fancy goldfish (fantails, ryukins, lionheads, telescopes and others) are slow, ornate forms of the goldfish that reach about 20 cm and live many years. One adult needs at least 100 litres and an 80 cm tank, plus about 50 litres for each extra fish, with a good filter and surface movement. Keep them with other fancies only: faster goldfish and fin-nippers out-eat them and damage their fins, and their fins are prone to fin rot. Coldwater: no heater is normally needed, never heat above 24 °C, and keep temperature changes to about 1 °C a day. Feed sinking food. Never release fish or fry into ponds or rivers; rehome them instead.

tank_mates.caution: Common, comet and shubunkin goldfish, which are faster, take the food and may nip fins; any fin-nipper; small fish; paradise fish, which may attack small fancies
tank_mates.good: Other fancy goldfish

It grows to about 12 cm, so give it at least 90 cm and 100 litres, with floating plants and open water at the surface, where it breathes air. Keep one male with two females, or a single fish. Tiger barbs and serpae tetras nip its long fins. Imported gouramis can carry an incurable virus: quarantine new fish on their own, choose active, well-coloured ones, and contact an aquatic vet if a new fish goes dark, stops eating or several die. Never release fish or fry; rehome them through a shop or club.

High bioload. Burrows; jumps; restless when air pressure changes. Established as an invasive in several European countries, Central Asia, the Philippines, the USA, Canada and Australia, largely through the aquarium trade (USGS, Seriously Fish). Paramisgurnus dabryanus is often sold under the same name (higher crest on the tail stalk, no dark spot at the top of the tail base) and is not on the EU list. Never release; not for outdoor ponds.
summary.guided: Never release it, and never keep it in an outdoor pond. This app describes the weather loach for keepers who already have one, but never suggests it for any tank, anywhere: it is banned in the EU, it has become an invasive pest in many countries after escaping or being released, and it grows to about 28 cm, too big for most aquariums. It is a cool-water fish from East Asia, best at 18–23 °C, so it does not belong in a heated tropical tank. It buries itself, so give it soft sand or fine gravel, and a tight lid, because it jumps. summary.expert: Sold as Micranthemum tweediei 'Monte Carlo' after a 2017 identification; Kew's checklist (WCVP) places M. tweediei under M. umbrosum, but the two grow very differently, so they are kept apart. Medium light, CO2 optional, medium growth, moderate (nursery Medium against Flowgrow easy). 1–5 cm (a shop gives 1–3 cm). pH 5.0–7.0 (Flowgrow and Dennerle). 20–26 °C (Dennerle's own page); a shop thinks it may tolerate below 20 °C, untested. In the nursery's 2013 trial it carpeted with less light and CO2 than HC 'Cuba'; a rich substrate helps.
summary.guided: A bright green carpeting plant with small round leaves, and much easier than HC 'Cuba': it can carpet in medium light, and added CO2 helps but isn't essential. Plant small pieces a few centimetres apart and trim it often so the carpet stays flat. It can also grow on rock or wood if you use liquid fertiliser.

plants.planting_note: Plant only in a mature, stable, algae-free tank: the pale leaves are easily coated by algae. Trim and replant often. Never put plants, plant pieces or tank water into ponds, rivers, streams or outdoor drains. Seal trimmings in a bag and put them in household rubbish, and don't compost them where they could reach water.

Medium light, CO2 low (boosts growth and colour), fast, advanced. 20–28 °C (cooler is safer against algae), pH 5.0–7.5. 30–60 cm is an expert call (parent species' figure). High demand, fed from the water column. Colour needs about 100 µmol PAR or more. Buy by full name where other milfoils are banned.
summary.guided: A fine, feathery milfoil that grows fast and turns cream to almost white with reddish tips under strong light; in weaker light it stays green. The pale leaves catch algae easily, so add it only to a mature, stable tank with steady feeding.

plants.planting_note: Tie thin tufts to wood or stone, upright or flat; it grips with rhizoids and seldom needs retying. Keep it wet while handling: it dries out and turns brittle quickly. Never put plants, plant pieces or tank water into ponds, rivers, streams or outdoor drains. Seal trimmings in a bag and put them in household rubbish, and don't compost them where they could reach water.

summary.guided: A small, feathery, deep green moss that you tie to wood or stone. It grows slowly and needs more light than most mosses to look its best, so it is not a beginner's moss. Keep it wet while handling it, and feed the tank evenly to keep algae off it.

plants.planting_note: Trim regularly and replant the tops, which grow dense and strong; slower side shoots suit small tanks. Stands that are cut but never replanted turn woody. Seal trimmings in a bag and put them in household rubbish, and don't compost them where they could reach water. Spare plants can go to another keeper or back to a shop where passing them on is allowed; for plants restricted where you live, follow your local rules.

Dysophylla quadrifolia, Eusteralis quadrifolia), sold earlier as Pogostemon stellatus 'Octopus' and identified as a separate species in 2013; true P. stellatus is a different, demanding plant. summary.guided: A very easy, fast-growing stem plant with narrow leaves in star-like whorls, for the back of the tank. It grows in moderate light without added CO2 and suits new tanks and beginners. Trim it often and replant the tops to keep it dense.

plants.planting_note: Float it on calm water; strong surface flow pushes it under. Stronger light turns the leaves red-brown, and it needs plenty of nutrients in the water. Never put plants, plant pieces or tank water into ponds, rivers, streams or outdoor drains. Seal trimmings in a bag and put them in household rubbish, and don't compost them where they could reach water.

Never put plants, plant pieces or tank water into ponds, rivers, streams or outdoor drains. summary.expert: A narrow-leaved trade form of Rotala rotundifolia, named after a hamlet in Gia Lai province, Vietnam; the apostrophe in 'H'ra' can't go in the scientific name field. Medium light, CO2 optional, fast (Flowgrow; a shop agrees), moderate. 22–28 °C (Flowgrow, within the nursery's former card for the species, 18–30 °C); pH 5.0–7.5, an expert call taking the overlap of Flowgrow's 4.5–7.5 and that former card's 5–8. 3–20 cm as a creeper (nursery); Flowgrow gives 20–80 cm for upright stems. The species is listed as invasive (category 2) by the Florida Invasive Species Council, an advisory list, not a ban. It is sometimes sold as Rotala indica, a name that belongs to a different plant.
summary.guided: A fine-leaved stem plant that turns orange in good light. It grows fast and does better with some added CO2, though it doesn't strictly need it. In strong light it creeps and can form a low orange cushion; otherwise it grows as upright stems. It is a form of dwarf rotala, which has escaped into the wild in Florida, so never let trimmings reach natural water.

plants.planting_note: Plant as a group in a small tank or the midground; remove any shoot that reverts to the larger green form so the dwarf form keeps its shape. Never put plants, plant pieces or tank water into ponds, rivers, streams or outdoor drains. Seal trimmings in a bag and put them in household rubbish, and don't compost them where they could reach water.

summary.guided: A small floating fern with round, hairy leaves and trailing roots that shelter fry. It grows fast, so skim it regularly. Buy only plants labelled Salvinia minima: some plants sold under other salvinia names are a seriously invasive, banned species.

summary.expert: Pistia stratiotes. Medium light, fast growth, no CO2, high nutrient demand, moderate difficulty (Flowgrow). 22–30 °C preferred, 15–35 °C tolerated (USGS, Flowgrow); pH 5–8. Floating water-column feeder; spreads by runners. Rosettes 6–30 cm across in the wild, much smaller in aquaria. Never put plants, plant pieces or tank water into ponds, rivers, streams or outdoor drains.
summary.guided: A fast-growing floating plant with soft, velvety rosettes and long hanging roots. It needs an open top, warmth and strong light, and runners soon cover the surface, so thin it out often. In the wild it forms dense mats that shade out other plants. Never put plants, plant pieces or tank water into ponds, rivers, streams or outdoor drains.

plants.planting_note: Plant stems one at a time in a group with the lowest leaves removed, and replant trimmed tips. Stems grown above water at the nursery drop those leaves after planting, and feathery underwater leaves follow within a few weeks. Never put plants, plant pieces or water that contains them into ponds, rivers or other waterways.

summary.expert: Hygrophila difformis (syn. H. triflora, Synnema triflorum). Low light (nursery rating; Flowgrow says medium to high), no CO2, fast, easy. Tolerates 22–30 °C, best 24–28 °C; pH 5–9, best 6.0–7.5. 20–30 cm, background or midground; feeds from water and roots. summary.guided: One of the easiest stem plants: it grows fast in low light without added CO2. If the first leaves fall off after planting, the plant is switching to its underwater form, not dying. nodes.expert_note: One plant grower groups coatings as diatoms, green algae and red algae. A sudden increase in algae is, by one hobby magazine's account, the most visible sign of phosphate building up from neglect: check your water-change log. No algaecide or hydrogen peroxide is suggested: no veterinary source on algaecides in aquaria was found, so no dose can be given. Liquid carbon is not suggested either: no independent study of these products was found and their strength is not disclosed. Warm tanks are more prone to algae and need extra care with light and feeding (one plant grower); never cool the tank below what its fish need.
steps: Clean the glass when you see algae, with a pad made for glass, or a soft sponge for acrylic, which scratches easily.
Keep the tank out of direct sunlight and avoid very bright or long lighting; more than 10 hours a day encourages algae.
Don't overfeed, and don't keep more fish than the tank can take.
Follow your care plan's water changes: they remove the extra nutrients algae feed on.
Remove melted or dead leaves promptly.
Algae eaters such as snails and shrimp can help once the causes are fixed, but they don't fix them. Any animal you add must suit your tank: check it with the stocking and compatibility checks.
nodes.title: Algae coating glass, leaves or decor

steps: Keep going with the fishless cycling guide.
The tank is cycled when a 2 ppm dose of ammonia is gone within 24 hours, with nitrite at 0 and nitrate showing.
Before fish go in, stop dosing ammonia the day before, change water to lower nitrate, and check that ammonia and nitrite read 0.
Don't use ammonia-binding products while the tank cycles: they may slow it down.
nodes.title: This is cycling at work
nodes.why: Ammonia and nitrite rising and then falling is how a tank cycles: bacteria are growing to clear them. With no animals in the tank, the readings harm nothing.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today if fish gasp at the surface, lie still, stop eating or die.
nodes.expert_note: Thresholds follow PetMD's fish vet (H1-C24): change at NH3/NH4 > 0.1 mg/L, any NO2, or NO3 > 20 mg/L, ≤ 50% at once. Intensive management usually lasts 1 to 2 weeks (Merck owner edition). Binders are not used while cycling (H1-C19).
steps: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate every day or every other day.

Change water whenever ammonia is above 0.1 ppm, nitrite is above 0 or nitrate is above 20 ppm: up to half at once with dechlorinated water within 2 °C of the tank, or at most 15% a day if tap and tank pH differ by more than 0.5.
Feed lightly, but don't starve the fish to speed up cycling.
Add no more fish until ammonia and nitrite stay at 0, then add a few at a time over days to weeks.
Don't use ammonia-binding products while the tank cycles: they may slow it down.
nodes.title: Fish in a tank that hasn't cycled
nodes.why: The filter bacteria haven't grown yet, so the ammonia and nitrite the fish produce build up in the water.

nodes.act_fast: Move the fish to matched clean water, or call an aquatic vet today.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today if you can't move the fish to matched water.
nodes.expert_note: Applies below pH 7 with total ammonia above 5 mg/L (old tank syndrome). Vets advise moving the fish to matched water rather than a large change in place.
steps: Don't do a big water change in this tank.
Prepare clean, dechlorinated water matched to the tank's temperature and pH, and move the fish into it.
Contact an aquatic vet.
nodes.title: High ammonia with low pH
nodes.why: When pH has fallen below 7, most of the ammonia is in a less toxic form. A big water change raises the pH and can turn it back into toxic ammonia, which can kill the fish.

nodes.act_fast: Change up to half the water now.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today if fish gasp at the surface, lie still, stop eating or die.
nodes.expert_note: Emergency means un-ionised ammonia ≥ 0.05 mg/L by the EPA formula from your pH and temperature (H1-C03), or nitrite ≥ 0.5 mg/L (H1-C05). No salt is suggested: no vet source covers it for ornamental fish and invertebrates (H1-C06).
steps: Change up to half the water now with dechlorinated water within 2 °C of the tank. If your tap water's pH differs from the tank's by more than 0.5, change at most 15% a day instead, on following days.
Stop feeding, or feed much less, for 1 to 3 days (this harms only fry), then bring food back gradually.
Remove dead fish and any rotting food.
Add an air stone or more surface movement.
A conditioner that binds ammonia can protect fish for a day or so, but it doesn't replace the water change, and an ammonia test may still read positive after using one.
Check that the filter is running and that its media weren't rinsed under the tap.
Test ammonia and nitrite again tomorrow with a liquid kit, and keep changing water until both read 0.
Watch the fish for the next 2 weeks: after nitrite poisoning, deaths can continue and survivors catch infections more easily.
nodes.title: Ammonia or nitrite is harming the fish
nodes.why: Ammonia damages the gills, and nitrite stops the blood carrying oxygen, so fish can suffocate even in well-aerated water. At this level, or with these signs, act now.

steps: Change up to half the water today with dechlorinated water within 2 °C of the tank. If your tap water's pH differs from the tank's by more than 0.5, change at most 15% a day instead, on following days.
Stop feeding, or feed much less, for 1 to 3 days (this harms only fry), then bring food back gradually.
Test ammonia and nitrite again tomorrow with a liquid kit, and keep changing water until both read 0.
From now on, rinse filter media only in water taken from the tank, never under the tap.
Clean half the media at a time, and replace sponges or biological media only when they fall apart, a third or half at a time, at least 4 weeks apart.
Add no fish until ammonia and nitrite stay at 0.
nodes.title: The filter's bacteria were set back
nodes.why: Most of the bacteria that clear ammonia and nitrite live in the filter. Rinsing media under the tap, washing it too hard or replacing it all at once kills them, and the tank partly cycles again.

steps: Change up to half the water today with dechlorinated water within 2 °C of the tank. If your tap water's pH differs from the tank's by more than 0.5, change at most 15% a day instead, on following days.
Stop feeding, or feed much less, for 1 to 3 days (this harms only fry), then bring food back gradually.
Test ammonia and nitrite again tomorrow with a liquid kit, and keep changing water until both read 0.
Then feed once or twice a day, only what the fish eat within about 2 minutes, and remove leftovers.
Add new fish a few at a time, with days to weeks between them.
nodes.title: More waste than the filter is used to
nodes.why: Each increase in fish or food needs the filter bacteria to catch up, which takes time. Overfeeding is a common cause of rising ammonia.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today if fish gasp at the surface, lie still, stop eating or die.
steps: Change up to half the water today with dechlorinated water within 2 °C of the tank. If your tap water's pH differs from the tank's by more than 0.5, change at most 15% a day instead, on following days.
Stop feeding, or feed much less, for 1 to 3 days (this harms only fry), then bring food back gradually.
Remove dead fish and any rotting food.
Check that the filter is running and that its media weren't rinsed under the tap.
Test your tap water after adding conditioner. If your supply uses chloramine, breaking it releases ammonia; a conditioner that also binds ammonia can help while the filter catches up.
Test ammonia and nitrite again tomorrow with a liquid kit, and keep changing water until both read 0.
nodes.title: Find what is adding ammonia
nodes.why: In an established tank, ammonia and nitrite should always read 0. A reading means something is wrong: often too much food, something rotting, or a filter problem.

nodes.expert_note: The slime advice rests on one plant grower (tier 4) only. Feeding follows the decided feeding rule (H2-C14): the 2-minute amount is the RSPCA's lower bound, and Merck gives 1–2% of body weight a day for maintenance. No manual-removal step and no chemical treatment is suggested: no source covers removal for slime, and no veterinary source we found supports a chemical. With ammonia present, Merck advises stopping or sharply cutting feeding until it is corrected; with nitrite, food is withdrawn.
steps: Change up to half the water, never more at once. If your tap water's pH differs from the tank's by more than 0.5, make smaller changes and repeat them. Repeat until ammonia and nitrite read 0.
If pH is below 7 and ammonia is high, don't make a big change in the tank: move the fish to matched clean water or contact an aquatic vet.

If nitrite reads above 0, stop feeding until it reads 0. If only ammonia reads above 0, stop feeding or feed much less until it reads 0. Then bring food back gradually: once or twice a day, only what the fish eat within about 2 minutes, and remove leftovers.
Keep testing the water and follow your care plan's water changes.

nodes.act_fast: If ammonia or nitrite reads above 0 with fish in the tank, do a 30–50% water change with dechlorinated water and test again tomorrow. If tap and tank pH differ by more than 0.5, make smaller changes and repeat them; if pH is below 7 with high ammonia, move the fish to matched clean water or contact an aquatic vet instead.
steps: Test ammonia and nitrite today and log the results.
Feed lightly and remove anything uneaten within a few minutes; don't stop feeding altogether.
Avoid big water changes, chemical clarifiers and replacing filter media; they slow the cycle.
nodes.title: Bacterial bloom in a cycling tank
nodes.why: New tanks often turn milky as free-floating bacteria multiply faster than the filter colony can keep up. It often clears without treatment, sometimes in days and sometimes over a few weeks while the tank cycles. Your test results matter more than the calendar.

nodes.act_fast: Any ammonia or nitrite reading above 0 means something is wrong: change up to half the water with dechlorinated water, test again the next day and repeat until both read 0. If tap and tank pH differ by more than 0.5, make smaller changes and repeat them; if pH is below 7 with high ammonia, move the fish to matched clean water or contact an aquatic vet instead.
steps: Test ammonia and nitrite and log the results.
Feed lightly and remove anything uneaten within a few minutes; don't stop feeding altogether.
Leave the filter alone; next time rinse media in old tank water only.
nodes.title: Bacterial bloom after a disturbance
nodes.why: A deep clean, a filter rinse in tap water or a jump in fish load can upset the bacteria balance and release nutrients that feed a bloom.

nodes.act_fast: Fish gasping at the surface can mean low oxygen, but also nitrite or a gill problem: add surface movement or an air stone right away, test nitrite, and follow the gasping troubleshooter.
steps: Check behind decor and plants for anything dead or decaying.
Feed lightly and remove anything uneaten within a few minutes; don't stop feeding altogether.
Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate, and do a 25% water change.
nodes.title: Bacterial bloom from excess food or decay
nodes.why: In a settled tank, a sudden milky haze usually means extra waste: overfeeding, a dead fish or snail, or rotting plant leaves.

nodes.act_fast: In algae-rich water, oxygen is lowest just before dawn: watch for fish gasping at the surface early in the morning.
steps: Follow the green water troubleshooter: it covers light, sunlight and feeding.
nodes.title: Green water (free-floating algae)
nodes.why: Green water is a bloom of tiny algae floating in the water, not cloudiness from bacteria or debris. It has its own troubleshooter.

nodes.act_fast: If it has not cleared in three days, or fish seem stressed, test ammonia and nitrite in case something is decaying underneath.
steps: Leave the filter running and wait 24–48 hours.
Add a fine filter floss pad to speed up clearing.
Next time, rinse new substrate and pour water onto a plate or bag.
nodes.title: Disturbed substrate or debris
nodes.why: Fine dust from new substrate, sand or a rescape stays suspended until the filter catches it. It is not a water-quality problem.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the fish doesn't improve once the water and food are right.
steps: Do a partial water change of no more than half the water, with dechlorinated water at the same temperature, and repeat until ammonia and nitrite read 0.
Check the filter is running and was not cleaned in tap water.
Once the water is right, start again from the first question if the fish hasn't recovered.
nodes.title: Fix the water first
nodes.why: Poor water is the commonest cause of buoyancy problems, by a fish vet's account of goldfish and koi, so the water comes before anything else.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet: every case of dropsy needs a vet to find the cause.
steps: Follow the swollen fish troubleshooter.
nodes.title: Swelling with raised scales
nodes.why: A swollen body with scales standing out is dropsy, a sign of illness inside the fish, and it can upset how the fish floats.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet: spinning needs a vet to find the cause.
nodes.expert_note: Merck names streptococcal infection and ammonia problems among causes of spinning; test ammonia and pH first.
steps: Test ammonia and pH now, and correct any problem with a partial water change of no more than half the water.
Don't add shop medicines without a vet's advice.
Contact an aquatic vet.
nodes.title: Spinning or spiralling
nodes.why: Spinning, spiralling or losing balance can come from an infection or from an ammonia problem. Test the water first; a vet is needed to find an infection.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet: gas bubbles in the fins or gills need a vet to confirm the cause.
nodes.expert_note: Gas supersaturation causes bubbles in fins and gills, popeye and buoyancy problems (Merck; PetMD's fish vet). Known causes are leaking or cavitating pumps and hoses, sudden pressure or temperature changes, and well water drawn from depth. Whether warming cold tap water causes it in a home tank is untested.
steps: Check for the known causes: a pump, hose or filter fitting that leaks or draws in air, a recent sudden change in temperature or pressure, or well water.
Don't add shop medicines without a vet's advice.
Contact an aquatic vet.
nodes.title: Gas bubbles in the fins or gills
nodes.why: Tiny bubbles in the fins or gills point to gas bubble disease: the water holds more dissolved gas than it should, and this can also upset how the fish floats.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the fish doesn't improve once the water and food are right. Also contact a vet if sores appear on the back of a fish stuck at the surface.
nodes.expert_note: By one fish vet's estimate only about 1 in 10 goldfish buoyancy cases is a true swim bladder disorder; most relate to water, diet, upkeep or injury. X-rays tell a swim bladder problem from gas in the gut; vets can remove air or operate. External floats only from a vet. No veterinary source gives a fasting period.
steps: Switch to a food that sinks.
Spread the food out so the fish doesn't have to compete for it.
Shelled green peas are one food a fish vet mentions as an option.
Keep the water very clean.
nodes.title: Goldfish floating at the top
nodes.why: Goldfish and koi fill their swim bladder by gulping air at the surface, so floating food and a scramble at feeding time can leave them floating. Fancy goldfish have little room for their swim bladder and are especially prone to this.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the fish doesn't improve once the water and food are right.
nodes.expert_note: By one fish vet's estimate only about 1 in 10 goldfish buoyancy cases is a true swim bladder disorder; most relate to water, diet, upkeep or injury. X-rays tell a swim bladder problem from gas in the gut; vets can remove air or operate. External floats only from a vet. No veterinary source gives a fasting period.
steps: Feed floating pellets rather than flakes.
Keep the water very clean.
Give it a smooth, bare bottom to rest on.
nodes.title: Goldfish sinking to the bottom
nodes.why: A fish that sinks may have a buoyancy problem from its diet or body shape; fancy goldfish are most at risk.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if sores appear on the back, or to ask about treatment: vets can X-ray the fish and sometimes remove air or repair the swim bladder.
nodes.expert_note: By one fish vet's estimate only about 1 in 10 goldfish buoyancy cases is a true swim bladder disorder; most relate to water, diet, upkeep or injury. X-rays tell a swim bladder problem from gas in the gut; vets can remove air or operate. External floats only from a vet. No veterinary source gives a fasting period.
steps: Give a bare or smooth bottom.
Keep the water very clean.
Hand-feed the fish if it struggles to reach food.
Check a fish stuck at the surface regularly for sores on its back, which is exposed to the air.
nodes.title: Living with a lasting buoyancy problem
nodes.why: Some fish, especially fancy goldfish, keep a buoyancy problem for life. Many live comfortably with a few changes.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the water and food are right and the betta still lies on the bottom or won't rise to eat.
steps: Check the betta lives in a heated, filtered tank, not a bowl.
Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate, and correct any problem with a partial water change of no more than half the water.
Check the food is fresh: use food opened within the last 6 months.
nodes.title: A betta lying on the bottom
nodes.why: True sinking problems are rare in bettas. A betta on the bottom is more often unwell from something else, or simply resting: bettas are naturally inactive. A healthy betta rises readily to eat.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the fish doesn't improve once the water and food are right.
steps: Keep the water very clean: test again and correct any problem.
Note what you see, and since when, to tell the vet.
Don't add shop medicines without a vet's advice.
nodes.title: Buoyancy problem in another kind of fish
nodes.why: The veterinary sources we found cover buoyancy problems in goldfish, koi and bettas only. In other fish the cause can't be narrowed down at home, so the water comes first, then a vet.

nodes.text: Look closely at the fish. Any spots, dust or extra slime on the body or fins, or flashing against decor?

nodes.act_fast: Any ammonia or nitrite reading means act today. Treat it as an emergency and change water now if nitrite is 0.5 mg/L or more, or if un-ionised ammonia is 0.05 mg/L or more (the toxic share of total ammonia, which rises in warm, alkaline water).
nodes.expert_note: Any measurable ammonia or nitrite means act today (H1-C03, H1-C05); it is an emergency from 0.05 mg/L un-ionised ammonia (EPA formula) or 0.5 mg/L nitrite. Ammonia toxicity rises with pH and temperature.
steps: Change up to half the water today, with dechlorinated water at the same temperature. If your tap water's pH differs from the tank's by more than 0.5, make smaller changes and repeat them.
If pH is below 7 and ammonia is high, don't make a big change in the tank: move the fish to matched clean water or contact an aquatic vet.
Skip feeding today, then feed lightly until readings are 0.
Test again tomorrow and repeat the water change until both read 0.
Check the filter is running and was not cleaned in tap water.
nodes.title: Ammonia or nitrite poisoning
nodes.why: Ammonia and nitrite damage the gills and stop blood carrying oxygen, so fish struggle to breathe even in well-oxygenated water.

nodes.act_fast: If fish are lying on the bottom or dying, change 50% of the water now.
steps: Increase surface movement: raise the filter outlet or add an air stone.
Do a 30% water change with dechlorinated water at the same temperature.
Get a liquid test kit, or ask a fish shop to test a sample today.
nodes.title: Treat as low oxygen until you can test
nodes.why: Without a test you can't tell poisoning from low oxygen, but the first steps help with both.

nodes.act_fast: Gasping with CO2 on is urgent: switch it off before anything else.
nodes.expert_note: A drop checker (4 dKH reference) turning yellow suggests CO2 above the roughly 30 mg/L that planted-tank guides treat as the upper target; Merck's normal value for fish is below 12 mg/L. Injected CO2 is usually aimed at 15–30 mg/L, and the app never suggests going above 30. The checker lags by hours, so watch the fish rather than the colour.
steps: Turn off the CO2 now.
Aerate vigorously: add an air stone and turn up surface movement.
Switch the CO2 off at lights-out. When the fish recover, restart at a lower bubble rate and raise it slowly over days, watching the fish rather than the drop checker.
nodes.title: Too much CO2
nodes.why: Injected CO2 lowers pH and makes it harder for the fish's blood to carry oxygen, so they breathe fast at the surface.

nodes.act_fast: If fish are struggling badly, add an air stone and do a 30% water change now.
steps: Add surface movement: point the filter outlet at the surface or add an air stone.
If the tank is warmer than 28 °C, bring it down gradually, unless your fish need it warm: a sudden change of even a few degrees can weaken fish.
In a planted tank, oxygen is lowest just before dawn: check the fish early in the morning.
nodes.title: Low oxygen
nodes.why: Warm water holds less oxygen while warm fish need more, and a still surface lets little oxygen in. Bigger fish suffer first.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet: a skin and gill sample is the only way to name the cause. Contact one today if several fish are breathing fast or any have died.
nodes.expert_note: Trichodina, Chilodonella, costia (Ichthyobodo) and gill flukes all cause fast breathing, excess slime and flashing (Merck; UF/IFAS). A vet's skin and gill sample decides the treatment; no dose is given here.
steps: Test ammonia, nitrite and pH again and correct any problem.
Keep the water very clean and avoid crowding.
Don't add shop medicines without a vet's advice.
Add an air stone while you wait for the vet.
nodes.title: Slime or flashing with fast breathing
nodes.why: Extra slime, a greyish film or flashing together with fast breathing can mean parasites on the skin and gills, such as flukes, Trichodina or costia. They can't be told apart without a microscope.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today if several fish are breathing fast with no water problem. Otherwise contact one before using any medication if breathing does not improve within a day, if fish start dying, or if the gills look pale.
steps: Watch for other signs: flashing against decor, red or swollen gills, clamped fins, spots.
If you can see the gills, note their colour: brown gills are a sign of nitrite, so test nitrite again; pale gills need a vet.
Check for anything new: medication, cleaning products, sprays near the tank.
Do a 30% water change and add an air stone while you watch them.
nodes.title: Possible gill irritation or disease
nodes.why: When water quality and oxygen look fine, fast breathing can come from disease or irritation of the gills. White spot on the gills, velvet, gill flukes and columnaris can all affect the gills without leaving marks on the body; a vet can tell which from a gill sample.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if fish keep dying or many are breathing fast, and today if it looks like a gold or rusty dust.
steps: Follow the white spots troubleshooter.
Add an air stone while you work through it.
nodes.title: Spots or dust with fast breathing
nodes.why: White spot and velvet both attack the gills as well as the skin, so fish breathe fast. A fine gold or rusty dust may be velvet, which needs a vet.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the fish gets worse or other fish fall ill once the water is right.
steps: If ammonia or nitrite reads above 0, open the ammonia and nitrite troubleshooter.
Bring pH and temperature back within the species' page gradually, never in one big step: no more than about 1 °C an hour.

nodes.title: The water is stressing it
nodes.why: Poor or unsuitable water is one of the commonest stresses. Ammonia makes fish sluggish and stop eating, and pH or temperature outside a species' range weakens it.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the fish keeps getting worse, or fish keep dying despite a properly given treatment.
steps: Open the troubleshooter that matches what you see.
nodes.title: A sign to follow up
nodes.why: Spots, dust, tufts, sores and ragged fins have their own causes, and each has its own troubleshooter. Most signs have several causes.

nodes.act_fast: Add surface movement and test the water now.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today if breathing doesn't improve once the water is right.
steps: Open the gasping troubleshooter.
nodes.title: A breathing problem
nodes.why: Fast breathing has water causes first, such as low oxygen or nitrite, but gill parasites can also cause it with no spots visible on the body.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet: swelling with raised scales has many causes and can need antibiotics.
steps: Open the troubleshooter that matches what you see.
nodes.title: A body or buoyancy problem
nodes.why: A swollen body, raised scales or trouble staying level have their own troubleshooters.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if wounds don't heal.
steps: Move the fish to a separate tank if you have one, or move the bully.
Check on each species' page that the fish suit each other and your tank.
Watch for ragged fins or sores.
nodes.title: Bullied by other fish
nodes.why: Aggression and territorial fights are a major stress, and a fish that is chased often hides and stops eating. Damaged skin also lets infections in.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if signs of illness appear or the fish gets worse.
steps: Keep the lights low and the tank quiet, and watch the fish closely for the first week.
Offer a small amount of food suited to the species, and remove what isn't eaten.
Keep testing the water: adding fish disturbs the tank for a while.
nodes.title: Settling in
nodes.why: Catching, handling, transport and new water are all major stresses, and new fish often hide and eat little at first. A stressed fish can look normal for a while, then fail suddenly, so watch it.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the fish gets worse or other signs appear.
steps: Check the heater and thermometer.
Bring the temperature back within the species' page by no more than about 1 °C an hour.
Make new water within 2 °C of the tank at every water change.
Watch for white spots over the next few weeks.
nodes.title: A sudden temperature change
nodes.why: Fish take the water's temperature. A sudden cold drop slows their immune system, and in one study immunity took up to 5 weeks to recover; white spot outbreaks often follow fast temperature changes.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the fish gets worse, other signs appear, or fish start dying.
steps: Keep the water clean and stable, and test it every few days.
Feed a good diet suited to the species, and remove what isn't eaten.
Look at the fish every day for the signs in this troubleshooter: spots, fast breathing, swelling or ragged fins.
nodes.title: No clear cause yet
nodes.why: Loss of appetite, hiding and sitting on the bottom are early signs that fit many causes. A stressed fish can look normal for a while, then fail suddenly.

nodes.text: Is the water itself green, or only the glass, plants and decor?
Does this tank have live plants?

nodes.act_fast: Algae-rich water is lowest in oxygen just before dawn. If fish gasp at the surface early in the morning, add an air stone and follow the gasping troubleshooter.
nodes.expert_note: Causes (one plant grower): excess nutrients, overfeeding and overstocking, more than 10 hours of light, direct sun, a faulty timer. The same grower suggests a 2–3 day blackout (tank covered, lights off); no source covers its effect on fish or on plants that need light, and injected CO2 should be off during it (an inference from how CO2 builds up when plants stop photosynthesising). The grower does not recommend UV sterilisers as a standard aid, because UV also kills useful bacteria. No algaecide or hydrogen peroxide is suggested: no veterinary source on algaecides in aquaria was found, so no dose can be given. Liquid carbon is not suggested either: no independent study of these products was found and their strength is not disclosed. Warm tanks are more prone to algae and need extra care with light and feeding (one plant grower); never cool the tank below what its fish need.
steps: Keep the tank out of direct sunlight.
Put the light on a timer and check it works. A new planted tank needs about 6 hours a day for its first 2 to 3 weeks, then 6 to 8 hours; more than 10 hours encourages algae.
Feed less: once or twice a day, only what the fish eat within about 2 minutes, and remove leftovers.
Let your test readings and care plan guide water changes; repeated water changes help clear green water.
Remove melted or dead leaves promptly.
Once the causes are fixed, a filter with plenty of fine filter material can help clear the water.
nodes.title: Green water in a planted tank
nodes.why: Green water is a bloom of tiny algae floating in the water. It usually follows too many nutrients in the water, from overfeeding or too many fish, together with too much light: long hours, direct sun or a faulty timer.

nodes.act_fast: Algae-rich water is lowest in oxygen just before dawn. If fish gasp at the surface early in the morning, add an air stone and follow the gasping troubleshooter.
nodes.expert_note: Causes (one plant grower): excess nutrients, overfeeding and overstocking, more than 10 hours of light, direct sun, a faulty timer. The same grower suggests a 2–3 day blackout (tank covered, lights off); no source covers its effect on fish or on plants that need light, and injected CO2 should be off during it (an inference from how CO2 builds up when plants stop photosynthesising). The grower does not recommend UV sterilisers as a standard aid, because UV also kills useful bacteria. No algaecide or hydrogen peroxide is suggested: no veterinary source on algaecides in aquaria was found, so no dose can be given. Liquid carbon is not suggested either: no independent study of these products was found and their strength is not disclosed. Warm tanks are more prone to algae and need extra care with light and feeding (one plant grower); never cool the tank below what its fish need.
steps: Keep the tank out of direct sunlight.
Put the light on a timer so it isn't left on for long hours, and avoid very bright lighting.
Feed less: once or twice a day, only what the fish eat within about 2 minutes, and remove leftovers.
Let your test readings and care plan guide water changes; repeated water changes help clear green water.
Remove melted or dead leaves promptly.
Once the causes are fixed, a filter with plenty of fine filter material can help clear the water.
nodes.title: Green water
nodes.why: Green water is a bloom of tiny algae floating in the water. It usually follows too many nutrients in the water, from overfeeding or too many fish, together with too much light: long hours, direct sun or a faulty timer.

steps: Follow the algae on glass and plants troubleshooter.
nodes.title: Algae on surfaces, not green water
nodes.why: If the water is clear and only the glass, plants or decor are green or brown, it is a coating of algae, which has its own troubleshooter.

nodes.expert_note: The plant grower sorts nuisance algae into green water, thread and hair algae, and coatings (diatoms, green and red algae, and blue-green slime, which usually follows overfeeding). No identification key from a tier 1–3 source was found.
steps: If the water itself is green or cloudy, open the cloudy water troubleshooter.
Use a timer and keep the tank out of direct sun. In a planted tank, light it 6 hours a day for the first 2–3 weeks, then 6–8 hours; more than 10 hours encourages algae.
Feed once or twice a day, only what your fish eat within about 2 minutes, and remove leftovers.
Don't use algae killers or liquid carbon products.
nodes.title: A different kind of algae
nodes.why: Green water, slimy coatings and spots are different groups of algae with their own causes, so this troubleshooter doesn't fit them.

nodes.expert_note: More than 10 hours of light a day often increases algae (plant grower). The plant grower's remedy for thread algae is more frequent water changes for a while (its algae pages give 30% every second day) plus algae-eating shrimp; in the app your readings set the interval. Dark tufted (black beard) algae gets the same balance checks as other algae, as the owner decided.
steps: Put the light on a timer and check that it switches when it should. In a planted tank, 6–8 hours of light a day is enough.
Shade the tank or move it so direct sun doesn't reach it.
Wind loose threads onto a rough stick and lift them out. Remove dead and melting leaves, and cut off leaves that are badly covered.
Do a water change now, then follow your care plan: your test readings decide how often, and change no more than 50% at once.
Don't use algae killers, hydrogen peroxide or liquid carbon products: no safe dose for fish and shrimp has been established.

Once the cause is fixed, algae-eating shrimp such as Amano shrimp can help graze thread algae; check that they suit your tank and fish first. Algae-eating fish need their own tank-size and group checks: see their species pages.
If fish start gasping at the surface after a lot of algae dies, open the gasping troubleshooter: decaying algae uses oxygen.
nodes.title: Too much light
nodes.why: Light that stays on for more than 10 hours, direct sun, or a timer that has failed gives algae more light than the plants can use.

nodes.why: Food the fish don't eat, and the waste of a crowded tank, release nutrients faster than the plants can use them. The plant grower calls this the most common cause of algae.

nodes.title: Warm water
nodes.why: Water above about 26 °C is one of the causes of algae the plant grower lists. Your fish's needs come first, so the answer is extra care with light and feeding, not cooling the tank.

nodes.why: When light, CO2 and nutrients are out of balance, algae uses what the plants can't. No single nutrient is to blame.
