nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if more fish die: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call. A vet's post-mortem of a fish that died can find diseases quarantine can't reveal, such as fish TB or neon tetra disease.
steps: Test ammonia and nitrite now. If either reads above 0, open the ammonia and nitrite troubleshooter.
Follow its result for fish in a tank that hasn't cycled: test every day or two and change water when ammonia or nitrite shows.
Add no more fish until ammonia and nitrite have stayed at 0.
For a future tank, finish cycling before any fish go in.
nodes.title: The tank hadn't finished cycling
nodes.why: Without enough filter bacteria, waste from the new fish builds up as ammonia and nitrite, which damage the gills and blood.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if more fish die: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call. A vet's post-mortem of a fish that died can find diseases quarantine can't reveal, such as fish TB or neon tetra disease.
steps: Test ammonia and nitrite now. If either reads above 0, open the ammonia and nitrite troubleshooter.
Feed lightly until ammonia and nitrite are back at 0.
Add the next group only when ammonia and nitrite have stayed at 0 for 14 days.
Build the tank gradually: one shoal of a single species first, then other groups one at a time.
nodes.title: Too many new fish at once
nodes.why: Each new batch of fish needs the filter bacteria to catch up. Adding too many too fast causes new tank syndrome even in a cycled tank.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if more fish die: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call. A vet's post-mortem of a fish that died can find diseases quarantine can't reveal, such as fish TB or neon tetra disease.
steps: Test ammonia and nitrite now. If either reads above 0, open the ammonia and nitrite troubleshooter. Bag water may have gone into the tank.
Keep the lights off for the rest of the day, and watch the remaining fish closely for the first week.

Next time follow the acclimation guide: lights off, float the closed bag for 20 to 30 minutes, mix in tank water only if the shop's pH differs from yours by more than 0.5, then net the fish across and throw the bag water away (never into the wild).
nodes.title: A shock on the way in
nodes.why: A sudden change of even a few degrees weakens fish. Bag water also gains ammonia and CO2 on the journey, and once the bag is opened that ammonia becomes more harmful.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if more fish die: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call. A vet's post-mortem of a fish that died can find diseases quarantine can't reveal, such as fish TB or neon tetra disease.
steps: Open the troubleshooter that matches the sign: white spots, ragged fins or gasping.
Don't add a general medicine without knowing the cause.
Remove dead fish promptly.
Next time, keep new fish in a separate quarantine tank for at least 4 weeks (30 days), longer if anything looks wrong.
nodes.title: An infection the fish brought with them
nodes.why: New fish often pass through several dealers, and parasite and bacterial infections are common in their first weeks. Healthy-looking fish can carry white spot and flukes, and white spot can show 1 to 3 weeks after arrival.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if more fish die: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call. A vet's post-mortem of a fish that died can find diseases quarantine can't reveal, such as fish TB or neon tetra disease.
steps: Move fish that are being chased or injured to a separate tank if you have one.
Check on each species' page that the fish suit each other and your tank.
When adding fish to a tank with territorial fish, rearrange the decor while the bag floats, and feed the residents as the newcomers go in.
Watch injured fish for ragged fins or sores.
nodes.title: Attacked by the fish already there
nodes.why: Aggression and territorial fights are a major stress for fish, and newcomers are easy targets. Damaged skin also lets infections in.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if more fish die: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call. A vet's post-mortem of a fish that died can find diseases quarantine can't reveal, such as fish TB or neon tetra disease.
steps: Test ammonia, nitrite, pH and temperature, and check they suit the species on its page.
Keep the lights off for the rest of the day the fish arrive, and watch them closely for the first week.
Remove dead fish promptly.
Next time, keep new fish in a separate quarantine tank for at least 4 weeks (30 days), longer if anything looks wrong.
nodes.title: Weak from the journey
nodes.why: Catching, handling, transport and new water are all major stresses. A stressed fish can look normal for a while as it uses up its reserves, then fail suddenly, and infections are common in the first weeks after arrival.

nodes.expert_note: Air leaves are thick and waxy with stomata; submerged leaves are thin with little cuticle (van Veen and Sasidharan 2019). No source compares how much lab-grown and air-grown plants melt.
steps: Leave the plant where it is: moving it again sets it back.
Remove melted leaves at their base, and leave the roots where they are.
Expect new leaves within a few weeks while the roots are healthy.
Plants grown in a laboratory (sold in small cups of gel) carry smaller reserves, so start fertilising them sooner.
Melting leaves release nutrients that can feed algae. Fast-growing stem plants or floating plants help use them up.
nodes.title: Leaves grown out of water are being replaced
nodes.why: Most nursery plants are grown with their leaves in air. Underwater the plant makes thinner leaves and drops the old ones, which yellow, turn see-through and dissolve. Cryptocoryne and Bucephalandra are especially prone.

steps: Keep conditions steady from now on, and make any further changes to light, fertiliser or CO2 gradually.
Remove melted leaves at their base, and leave the roots where they are.
Wait at least 3 to 4 weeks for new shoots before you move or replace the plant.
Melting leaves release nutrients that can feed algae. Fast-growing stem plants or floating plants help use them up.
nodes.title: A sudden change set the plant back
nodes.why: Established plants, Cryptocoryne most of all, can melt after being moved or after sudden changes in light, fertiliser, CO2, water changes or temperature.

nodes.expert_note: The app doesn't recommend liquid carbon products (H8-C05).
steps: Stop dosing the product.
Remove melted leaves at their base, and leave the roots where they are.
Keep conditions steady and wait for new growth.
Melting leaves release nutrients that can feed algae. Fast-growing stem plants or floating plants help use them up.
nodes.title: Damage from liquid carbon
nodes.why: The maker of a liquid carbon product says large doses can melt Vallisneria, and that anacharis-type plants are particularly sensitive.

steps: Check the plant's page. If it needs CO2 or strong light that your tank doesn't have, swap it for an easier plant.
Trim taller plants that shade smaller ones.
Fertilise as the fertilising guide describes for your tank.
Remove melted leaves at their base, and leave the roots where they are.
nodes.title: Not enough light, nutrients or CO2
nodes.why: A plant short of light or nutrients gives up its older leaves first, so they yellow and drop. Small plants shaded by bigger ones, and demanding plants in tanks without CO2 and strong light, suffer most.

options.label: A clear or white edge

options.hint: Or there are sores or red streaks on the body
options.label: The rot has reached the body

nodes.text: Look closely at the edge of the damaged fin. What do you see?

options.label: Ammonia or nitrite above 0, or nitrate high

nodes.text: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate now. What do they read?

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the edge is still red after a week of good water, if the rot reaches the body, or if several fish are affected. A vet can treat an infection that persists, for example with injected antibiotics; shop fin rot medicines are not advised because they barely reach the fin edge and can harm the filter.
steps: Do a partial water change of no more than half the water, with dechlorinated water at the same temperature.
Test daily and repeat until ammonia and nitrite read 0.
Check the filter is running and was not cleaned in tap water.
Then follow the injury steps: remove sharp decor and nippy tank mates.
nodes.title: Fin damage made worse by water quality
nodes.why: Fin rot usually starts with a small injury that bacteria in the water infect. Poor water slows healing and lets the infection spread, so the water comes first.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the edge is still red after a week of good water, if the rot reaches the body, or if several fish are affected. A vet can treat an infection that persists, for example with injected antibiotics; shop fin rot medicines are not advised because they barely reach the fin edge and can harm the filter.
nodes.expert_note: Vets rarely recommend antibiotics for fin rot: they barely reach the fin edges, and in-water treatments can wipe out the filter bacteria.
steps: Remove sharp decor and plastic plants, or swap them for smooth or live ones.
Check for fin-nipping tank mates and separate them if needed.
Give long-finned fish smooth places to rest.
Keep the water clean, warm and stable, and feed a good varied diet.
Don't add shop fin rot medicines; watch the fin edge every day.
nodes.title: Fin injury with infection
nodes.why: With clean water, the usual cause is an injury: snagging on sharp decor or plastic plants, or nipping by tank mates. Long-finned fish such as bettas, fancy guppies and fancy goldfish are most at risk. Recovery depends on the fish's own immune system, so the fix is removing the cause and keeping the water clean.

nodes.escalate: If the edge turns red or ragged again, start from the first question.
steps: No treatment is needed.
Keep the water clean and remove whatever caused the damage.
nodes.title: Fins growing back
nodes.why: A clear or white edge is usually new fin tissue growing back, which is often mistaken for fin rot.

nodes.act_fast: Get advice today.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today.
steps: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate and correct any problem.
Look over the body for sores, ulcers or red streaks and take clear photos.
Contact an aquatic vet today.
nodes.title: Infection spreading to the body
nodes.why: Rot that reaches the body, or sores, ulcers and red streaks, means the infection is no longer only at the fin edge. Treat it as a body infection, not as fin rot.

options.hint: Fish that hunt shrimp, crayfish, large prawns or crabs, or hydra, planaria or leeches seen
options.label: Yes, or shrimp seem to be going missing

options.label: Food is still there after a few hours

Amano shrimp kept 2 years or more

nodes.text: How long have you kept these shrimp?

options.label: The new water was untreated, or differed from the tank

nodes.text: Test the tank now for ammonia, nitrite, pH, temperature, GH and KH. If you changed water, test the new water as well. What do you find?

options.label: Turning pink or white, losing balance, trying to leave the water, or lying still with twitching legs
A pale band behind the head, or stuck in the old shell

nodes.text: Look at the shrimp that are still alive. Do any of these fit?

steps: Leave the shell in the tank: the shrimp eat it.
The shrimp hides until its new shell hardens, so don't worry if you see less of it for a while.
nodes.title: A moult, not a death
nodes.why: Shrimp shed their shell to grow. A cast shell is clear, empty and split along the back; a dead shrimp is opaque all through.

nodes.expert_note: Cards keep 4 dGH as the lower limit (H7-C01); failed moults are the reason to aim for 6 to 8. No source sets how fast to raise GH. Keepers also blame GH that is too high, protein-rich food and water changes, but no source supports these.
steps: Check GH against the species' page.
If it is low, raise it gradually: add a shrimp mineral product to the water-change water, mixed to a GH you have tested, aiming for 6 to 8 dGH for cherry and Amano shrimp.
Feed foods that contain calcium.
Leave cast shells in the tank.
Never use raw reverse-osmosis water.
nodes.title: Failed moults
nodes.why: A shrimp that dies with a pale band behind its head, or stuck in its old shell, died while moulting. The new shell is hardened partly with calcium from the water, so soft water is the usual cause.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if three or more shrimp die within a week with normal water readings and no clear cause. One death or an empty moult is not a reason to call.
steps: If ammonia and nitrite read 0, don't make another large change now: it could be a second shock.
Always use a conditioner that treats chloramine.
Make the next change with water dechlorinated, within 2 °C of the tank and remineralised to its GH and KH.
If tap and tank pH differ by more than 0.5, change at most 15% a day instead, on following days.
Test the new water before it goes in.
Never use raw reverse-osmosis water.
nodes.title: Shocked by the new water
nodes.why: Sudden changes in temperature or water values can kill shrimp quickly, so deaths after a water change usually point to new water that differed from the tank's.

nodes.act_fast: Change water now, with water matched to the tank.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if three or more shrimp die within a week with normal water readings and no clear cause. One death or an empty moult is not a reason to call.
steps: If pH is below 7 and ammonia is above 5 ppm, don't make a big change: move the shrimp to clean water matched for temperature and pH, or contact an aquatic vet.
Otherwise change up to half the water now, with water dechlorinated, within 2 °C of the tank and remineralised to its GH and KH.
If tap and tank pH differ by more than 0.5, change at most 15% a day instead, on following days.
Feed less and remove leftovers.
Remove dead shrimp and anything rotting.
Test again tomorrow and repeat until both read 0.
Never add shrimp to a tank that hasn't finished cycling.
nodes.title: Ammonia or nitrite
nodes.why: Dwarf shrimp are very sensitive to ammonia and nitrite, which damage the gills and the blood's ability to carry oxygen. In an established tank both should read 0.

nodes.act_fast: Remove the source and change water now.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if three or more shrimp die within a week with normal water readings and no clear cause. One death or an empty moult is not a reason to call. If many shrimp die at once, keep a few freshly dead ones chilled, with a water sample, in case a vet or laboratory can test them.
nodes.expert_note: In a laboratory test, imidacloprid reduced movement in Neocaridina from 0.031 mg/L (Siregar 2021); the dose on a bought plant is unknown. Some shrimp specialists hold bought plants for several weeks, but no safe time has been tested (H7-C24). No source says whether carbon removes plant pesticides.
steps: Take the new plants out, or stop using sprays and cleaning products near the tank.
Change up to half the water now, with water dechlorinated, within 2 °C of the tank and remineralised to its GH and KH.
There is no cure for shrimp already showing these signs.

In future, choose plants grown in a laboratory (sold in small cups of gel), or keep bought plants in a separate container for at least a few days and rinse them well. Rinsing isn't proven to remove pesticides.
nodes.title: Poisoning from plants or sprays
nodes.why: New plants can carry insecticides that kill shrimp, and sprays or cleaning products near the tank can poison them too. Poisoned shrimp turn pink or white, lose balance, try to leave the water, or lie still with twitching legs.

nodes.act_fast: Stop dosing and change water now.
nodes.escalate: If fish need treating and the shrimp can't be moved out first, contact an aquatic vet before dosing. If many shrimp die at once, keep a few freshly dead ones chilled, with a water sample, in case a vet or laboratory can test them.
steps: Stop dosing.
Change up to half the water with water dechlorinated, within 2 °C of the tank and remineralised to its GH and KH, add carbon to the filter to remove the medicine, and add aeration.
In future, move shrimp to another tank before any medicine goes in, and keep copper out until a test reads 0.
If your water comes through copper pipes, run the cold tap for a while before drawing water.
nodes.title: Medicine, copper or salt
nodes.why: Copper at fish-treatment levels kills shrimp, and many fish medicines, algae products and snail killers contain copper or other substances that harm invertebrates. Salt at fish 'tonic' levels can kill adult Amano shrimp.

nodes.act_fast: Add surface movement now.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if three or more shrimp die within a week with normal water readings and no clear cause. One death or an empty moult is not a reason to call.
steps: Add an air stone or more surface movement.
If the water is warmer than the species' page allows, bring it down gradually.
Turn injected CO2 off until the shrimp recover.
After a power cut, check that the filter and heater are running again.
nodes.title: Too little oxygen
nodes.why: Warm water holds less oxygen, oxygen is lowest before dawn in planted tanks, and a still surface or a power cut lets it fall. Injected CO2 makes it harder for the blood to carry oxygen.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if three or more shrimp die within a week with normal water readings and no clear cause. One death or an empty moult is not a reason to call.
steps: Keep the tank's readings within the species' page.
Keep new shrimp out of tanks with fish or other animals that hunt them.
Buy captive-bred shrimp where they exist.
nodes.title: Stress from transport and the shop
nodes.why: Many shop shrimp are wild-caught and imported, shipped crowded in poor water and then kept in unsuitable water, and adults are of unknown age. This leaves them weak and slow to adapt.

steps: Check each animal's page for whether it eats shrimp.
Keep a breeding colony in its own tank with dense plants.
Cover the filter intake so baby shrimp aren't sucked in.
If you see hydra, planaria or leeches, open the small creatures troubleshooter.
nodes.title: Something is eating them
nodes.why: Almost all fish eat baby shrimp, and some fish, crayfish, large prawns, crabs, hydra, planaria and leeches kill adults. Newly moulted shrimp are the easiest prey, and eaten shrimp usually just go missing.

steps: Feed small amounts that are eaten within a few hours, and remove what is left.
Let a new tank mature, with surfaces that grow a film to graze, before adding filter-feeding shrimp or a breeding colony.
With Amano shrimp, give smaller shrimp food the Amanos can't take first.
nodes.title: Too much food, or the wrong kind of tank
nodes.why: Uneaten food turns into ammonia and feeds pests that eat baby shrimp. Filter-feeding shrimp starve in new, clean tanks, and Amano shrimp can take the food before smaller shrimp reach it.

nodes.expert_note: A specialist gives two to three years for most dwarf shrimp; Amano keepers report up to four years and sometimes eight or more (H7-C25, H7-C26).
steps: Keep the water stable and within the species' page so the colony keeps breeding.
Keep feeding and testing as usual.
nodes.title: Probably old age
nodes.why: Shrimp are short-lived: dwarf shrimp about one to two years, less in warm tanks, and Amano shrimp several years. A slow trickle of deaths in a colony that keeps breeding can be normal.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if three or more shrimp die within a week with normal water readings and no clear cause. One death or an empty moult is not a reason to call. If many shrimp die at once, keep a few freshly dead ones chilled, with a water sample, in case a vet or laboratory can test them.
steps: Don't make a large water change while readings are normal.
Remove dead shrimp promptly.
Test again over the next few days, and watch for pink or white shrimp, failed moults or shrimp going missing.
Check what has been near the tank: sprays, cleaning products, new plants or decor.
nodes.title: No clear cause yet
nodes.why: Your readings are within the species' page and nothing obvious changed, so the cause isn't clear yet.

provenance.change_note: New 2026-11-09 from the owner's reviewed h7-dying chapter and its proposed tree (h7-dying-tree), forum demand topic 28. Follows H7-C01, C02, C23 (no second large change when readings are normal), C24 (no tested holding time for plants), C25, C26 (Amano not offered old age under 2 years), C27 (vet at three or more deaths within a week with normal readings), H8-C13, H4-C03, H1-C15 and H2-C07. Uses the owner's 2026-11-09 expert calls: fast means several within a day or two, slow one now and then over weeks; the question asks about the last 2 weeks; missing shrimp suggest predators. The power-cut and copper-pipe steps rest on h7-dying-oxygen and h7-dying-copper (h2-power-after and h1-tap-other are not reviewed). Further expert calls proposed for the owner: 'dwarf shrimp kept a year or more' as the old-age prompt; 'bring it down gradually' for warm water; 'Cover the filter intake'; 'more than 2 °C, pH more than 0.5 apart, or clearly different GH or KH' as the mismatch test; 'keep a few chilled with a water sample' adapted from the fish advice. No treatment or medicine for shrimp is given. Draft until the owner signs it. Approved by Hooman in chat on 2026-11-09 after Claude summarised the shrimp troubleshooter and its five expert calls ("Sign it") and the Help order ("After sudden fish deaths").

Does the tank hold shrimp, eggs or fry?

Rounded, and the worm is very small

Does the tank hold shrimp, snails you want to keep, eggs or fry?

Is a leech attached to a fish?

nodes.text: Look at the rear end. Does it have three leaf-like tails?

nodes.expert_note: Stretched out they are about 1–5 cm; contracted, a speck. They multiply mainly by budding, and pull in when something comes close, which algae does not.
steps: Feed only what your fish eat within a couple of minutes.
Clean the gravel at your next water change to remove leftover food.
Siphon debris and remove decaying leaves.
Don't crush them on the glass.
They often fade as a new tank matures. No medicine is needed.
nodes.title: Hydra: harmless to adult fish
nodes.why: Hydra are small relatives of jellyfish that catch tiny animals with their tentacles. They live on the small creatures that leftover food supports, so they cannot harm adult fish.

nodes.escalate: If hydra keep killing fry or baby shrimp after you cut feeding, ask an aquatic vet or an experienced shrimp keeper before using any product.
steps: Feed only what your fish eat within a couple of minutes.
Clean the gravel at your next water change to remove leftover food.
Siphon debris and remove decaying leaves.
Move fry or eggs to a tank without hydra if you can.
Stop feeding live daphnia or baby brine shrimp into this tank for a while.

Products sold against planaria and hydra can kill snails and may kill shrimp, and no vet source supports using them for this. Move shrimp and snails to another tank before any medicine goes in, and ask an aquatic vet or specialist first. Never use copper.
nodes.title: Hydra: a risk to fry and baby shrimp
nodes.why: Hydra catch and eat very small animals, including fry and baby shrimp. Their numbers follow the tiny creatures that leftover food supports.

steps: Check the algae troubleshooter for what to do next.
nodes.title: Probably algae, not hydra
nodes.why: Hydra pull in when something comes close; algae and most other growths do not. A growth that doesn't react is most likely algae.

steps: Feed only what your fish eat within a couple of minutes.
Clean the gravel at your next water change to remove leftover food.
Trap them overnight with a little food in a trap or a jar, and throw the catch away.
No medicine is needed.
nodes.title: Planaria: harmless to adult fish
nodes.why: Planaria are flatworms that glide over the glass and feed on leftover food. Their numbers follow the food, and they don't harm adult fish.

nodes.escalate: Before using any planaria product, move shrimp and snails out and ask an aquatic vet or specialist.
nodes.expert_note: Wormers such as fenbendazole and flubendazole can kill any snail; nothing sold against planaria can be called shrimp safe, and praziquantel is not a safer choice. No product names or doses are given because no veterinary source covers these uses.
steps: Feed only what your fish eat within a couple of minutes.
Clean the gravel at your next water change to remove leftover food.
Trap them every night for several weeks: eggs can hatch for up to about 7 weeks.
Remove whole worms. Never cut them: pieces can grow into new worms.

Products sold against planaria and hydra can kill snails and may kill shrimp, and no vet source supports using them for this. Move shrimp and snails to another tank before any medicine goes in, and ask an aquatic vet or specialist first. Never use copper.
nodes.title: Planaria: a risk to eggs, fry, baby shrimp and small snails
nodes.why: Planaria are flatworms that eat eggs, fry, baby shrimp and small snails. Their numbers follow leftover food, and their eggs keep hatching for weeks.

steps: Feed only what your fish eat within a couple of minutes.
Clean the gravel at your next water change to remove leftover food.
Check the head shape again on another evening, when they are out on the glass.
nodes.title: Telling planaria from other worms
nodes.why: Planaria glide smoothly and have a triangular or arrow-shaped head with two dark eye dots. Worms that wriggle or thrash are round worms, which are usually harmless detritus worms.

steps: Feed only what your fish eat within a couple of minutes.
Clean the gravel at your next water change to remove leftover food.
nodes.title: Small round-headed flatworms: harmless
nodes.why: Very small flatworms with rounded heads are not planaria. They are harmless and live on leftover food.

steps: Feed only what your fish eat within a couple of minutes.
Clean the gravel at your next water change to remove leftover food.
Don't medicate: the worms are a sign, not the problem.
nodes.title: Detritus worms: harmless
nodes.why: These thin worms eat leftovers in the gravel, and fish eat them. Large numbers mean too much food or gravel that traps waste.

nodes.act_fast: If fish are gasping at the surface, increase surface movement and change water now.
steps: Test ammonia and nitrite today.
Increase surface movement with the filter outlet or an air stone.
Do a water change with dechlorinated water at the same temperature.
Skip feeding for a few days, then clean the gravel.
nodes.title: Worms in open water: check oxygen and waste
nodes.why: When many worms leave the gravel and swim in open water, the water may be short of oxygen or the substrate may hold decaying food.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet: treatment is a wormer given in food after a diagnosis.
steps: Note which fish are affected and how many.
Don't add new fish until a vet has seen the problem.
nodes.title: Worms coming from a fish: an internal parasite
nodes.why: Red or white threads hanging from a fish's vent are worms living inside the fish, often Camallanus. They are not tank pests and need a diagnosis.

steps: Pick out every leech you see.
Check again at night, and keep checking for several weeks.
Quarantine new plants and don't feed live food from ponds.

Products sold against planaria and hydra can kill snails and may kill shrimp, and no vet source supports using them for this. Move shrimp and snails to another tank before any medicine goes in, and ask an aquatic vet or specialist first. Never use copper.
nodes.title: Leeches: a risk to snails and shrimp
nodes.why: Most leeches in tanks hunt snails and shrimp. They come in on plants or with pond live food, and their eggs can hatch weeks later.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet for safe removal and to check the fish.
steps: Don't pull it off roughly.
Check the other fish for leeches.
nodes.title: A leech feeding on a fish
nodes.why: A leech attached to a fish feeds on its blood. It can cause anaemia and sores and can spread blood parasites.

steps: No action is needed.
Don't collect live food from ponds.
nodes.title: Tiny crustaceans: harmless
nodes.why: Seed shrimp, copepods and water fleas are tiny crustaceans that fish eat. Their numbers show there is plenty of food in the tank.

steps: Keep the fry tank clean.
Don't collect live food from ponds.
nodes.title: Tiny crustaceans in a fry tank
nodes.why: Seed shrimp, copepods and water fleas are harmless to most fish, but large numbers of copepods can attack very small fish larvae.

steps: No action is needed in a community tank.
Keep them out of breeding tanks: check plants before you move them in.
nodes.title: Scuds: harmless, except in breeding tanks
nodes.why: Scuds are small crustaceans that are harmless to fish, shrimp and snails. In a tank with eggs or fry they may eat eggs and very small young.

steps: Catch or siphon them out.
Check and quarantine new plants; prefer plants grown indoors.
Never use garden insect sprays.
nodes.title: Damselfly nymph: a risk to fry and small fish
nodes.why: Damselfly nymphs are insect larvae that hunt small animals. They can kill fry and very small fish; adult fish are not at risk.

steps: Catch or siphon them out.
Check and quarantine new plants; prefer plants grown indoors.
Never use garden insect sprays.
nodes.title: Dragonfly nymph: a risk to fry and small fish
nodes.why: Dragonfly nymphs are insect larvae that hunt small animals. They can kill fry and very small fish; adult fish are not at risk.

steps: Feed only what your fish eat within a couple of minutes.
Clean the gravel at your next water change to remove leftover food.
Remove snails by hand or siphon them out, or trap them overnight with a piece of vegetable or food as bait.
Keep new plants in a separate container for a while before they go in.
Don't use wormers or planaria products against snails: they kill the snails you want to keep too.
nodes.title: Lots of small snails
nodes.why: Small snails come in on plants and multiply when there is plenty of leftover food. They are a sign of overfeeding rather than a danger to fish.

nodes.text: Look closely at the fish still alive. What do you see?

nodes.act_fast: Change water now, then contact a vet today.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call a vet.
steps: Change up to half the water now with dechlorinated water at the same temperature. If your tap water's pH differs from the tank's by more than 0.5, do smaller changes and repeat them.
Stop feeding for a day or two; this harms only fry.
Remove dead fish and look for anything rotting.
Add an air stone or more surface movement.
Test again and repeat until ammonia and nitrite read 0. Check the filter is running and was not cleaned in tap water.
nodes.title: Ammonia or nitrite is harming the fish
nodes.why: Ammonia and nitrite damage the gills and blood. In an established tank either reading above 0 means something has gone wrong, such as overfeeding, a dead fish rotting out of sight, or a filter that has stopped working.

nodes.act_fast: Move the fish to matched clean water and contact a vet today.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call a vet.
nodes.expert_note: Applies below pH 7 with total ammonia above 5 mg/L (old tank syndrome). Vets advise moving the fish to matched water rather than a large change in place.
steps: Don't do a big water change in this tank.
Prepare clean, dechlorinated water matched to the tank's temperature and pH, and move the fish into it.
Contact an aquatic vet.
nodes.title: High ammonia with low pH
nodes.why: When pH has fallen below 7, most of the ammonia is in a less toxic form. A big water change raises the pH and can turn it back into toxic ammonia, which can kill the fish.

nodes.act_fast: Stop the medicine and change water now, then contact a vet today.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today, before giving any more medicine.
steps: Stop dosing.
Change up to half the water with dechlorinated water at the same temperature.
Add activated carbon to the filter to take the medicine out of the water.
Add an air stone or more surface movement.
Move any fish that dart, gasp or try to jump into clean, well-aerated water.
Check the dose you used against the label and the real amount of water in the tank.
nodes.title: Deaths after adding a medicine
nodes.why: Medicines given at too high a dose, or mixed with other products, can kill fish. Doses have to be worked out for the actual amount of water.

nodes.act_fast: Change water now, then contact a vet today.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call a vet.
steps: Stop using the chemical near the tank.
Change up to half the water with dechlorinated water at the same temperature.
Add an air stone or more surface movement.
Freeze a few freshly dead fish and a sample of tank water for testing.
Contact an aquatic vet: most fish laboratories test only basic water quality, not chemicals, so ask where to send samples.
nodes.title: Possible poisoning
nodes.why: Aerosol sprays, cleaning products, pesticides and other chemicals that reach a tank can poison fish by damaging their gills and skin.

nodes.act_fast: Start the white spots troubleshooter now.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call a vet.
steps: Follow the white spots troubleshooter now.
Remove dead fish promptly. Keep one that died within the last day in a sealed bag in the fridge, not the freezer, for the vet to examine.
nodes.title: Spots or dust on the survivors
nodes.why: White spot and velvet can both kill many fish quickly. Velvet looks like a fine gold or rusty dust and needs a vet.

nodes.act_fast: Start the gasping troubleshooter now.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call a vet.
steps: Follow the gasping troubleshooter now.
Remove dead fish promptly. Keep one that died within the last day in a sealed bag in the fridge, not the freezer, for the vet to examine.
nodes.title: Survivors breathing fast
nodes.why: Fish breathing fast after deaths may have damaged gills, low oxygen or a water problem.

nodes.act_fast: Contact a vet today.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call a vet, and a skin and gill sample is the only way to name the cause.
nodes.expert_note: Trichodina, Chilodonella, costia (Ichthyobodo) and flukes cause excess slime, flashing and fast breathing (Merck). A vet's skin and gill sample decides the treatment; no dose is given here.
steps: Remove dead fish promptly. Keep one that died within the last day in a sealed bag in the fridge, not the freezer, for the vet to examine.
Keep the water very clean and add an air stone or more surface movement.
Don't add shop medicines without a vet's advice.
nodes.title: Survivors flashing or slimy
nodes.why: Flashing, extra slime or a greyish film on the survivors can mean parasites on the skin and gills, such as flukes, Trichodina or costia. Some of them kill many fish, and they can't be told apart without a microscope.

nodes.act_fast: Contact a vet today.
nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet today: more than one unexplained death is a reason to call a vet.
nodes.expert_note: Fresh samples only: dead under 24 hours and chilled at about 4 °C straight away; frozen fish are of limited use and fish found floating are useless for diagnosis. Send at least 500 mL of tank water with the fish. Chronic wasting, ulcers that do not heal, or repeated deaths in one tank raise the question of fish TB, which can only be confirmed by examining a dead fish's organs. If fish TB is possible, ask a vet for a post-mortem of the next fish that dies; decide about the rest of the tank only once a diagnosis is confirmed, never on suspicion alone.
steps: Change up to half the water with dechlorinated water at the same temperature.
Add an air stone or more surface movement.
Stop feeding for a day; this harms only fry.
If the temperature is outside your fish's range, check the heater and bring it back gradually.
Remove dead fish promptly. Keep one that died within the last day in a sealed bag in the fridge, not the freezer, for the vet to examine.
Wear gloves when you work in the tank, wash your hands afterwards and keep tank water away from cuts: one possible cause, fish TB, can infect people through cuts and scratches.
Contact an aquatic vet.
nodes.title: Deaths with no clear cause
nodes.why: Fish can die from many causes that look alike from outside: infections, parasites, poisons or a problem you can't test for at home. A vet can examine a fresh fish and find the cause.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet: every case of dropsy needs a vet to find the cause.
nodes.expert_note: Causes named by fish vets: poor water, poor diet, bullying by tank mates, Aeromonas, mycobacteria, viruses (goldfish herpesvirus, spring viraemia of carp), heavy parasite loads, kidney or liver disease, tumours. A vet may examine fluid, blood, skin or gill samples or use imaging, and treats the cause; a vet may raise the salt level as part of treatment (salt is not for fish without true scales, invertebrates or planted tanks without a vet's advice). No veterinary source supports Epsom salt or shop antibiotics for dropsy. Early cases can improve over days to weeks; advanced cases may not. Fish TB is one possible cause; it can only be confirmed by examining a dead fish's organs, so tell the vet about any repeated deaths, wasting or ulcers that do not heal. If fish TB is possible, ask a vet for a post-mortem of the next fish that dies; decide about the rest of the tank only once a diagnosis is confirmed, never on suspicion alone.
steps: Do a partial water change of no more than half the water, with dechlorinated water at the same temperature, and repeat until ammonia and nitrite read 0.
If pH is below 7 and ammonia is very high, don't change a lot of water in place: move the fish to prepared water matched for temperature and pH, and contact an aquatic vet.

If you already have a hospital tank running with a mature filter, move the fish there so you can watch it. Don't set one up from scratch now: a new tank goes through its own ammonia rise, and handling stresses the fish. Otherwise leave it where it is.
Keep the water excellent: keep testing, and keep ammonia and nitrite at 0.
Watch the other fish closely for swelling, raised scales or other changes.
Don't add shop medicines without a vet's advice.
Wear gloves when you work in the tank, wash your hands afterwards and keep tank water away from cuts: one possible cause, fish TB, can infect people through cuts and scratches.
Contact an aquatic vet, who can examine the fish and look for the cause.
nodes.title: Dropsy, with a water problem
nodes.why: Scales standing out like a pinecone and a swollen body mean fluid is building up inside the fish, because its kidneys or gills can't remove water. That is a sign of an illness inside the fish, such as a bacterial infection, organ failure, fish TB, a virus or a tumour, not a disease in itself. Dropsy doesn't spread from fish to fish, but its cause might.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet about euthanasia.
nodes.expert_note: A fish vet lists terminal disease, decline and disease that does not respond to treatment among reasons to discuss euthanasia. If fish TB is possible, ask a vet for a post-mortem of the next fish that dies; decide about the rest of the tank only once a diagnosis is confirmed, never on suspicion alone.
steps: Contact an aquatic vet and talk about whether treatment is still possible, or whether to put the fish to sleep.
Test the water and correct any problem for the other fish's sake, and watch them closely.
Wear gloves when you work in the tank, wash your hands afterwards and keep tank water away from cuts: one possible cause, fish TB, can infect people through cuts and scratches.
nodes.title: A swollen fish that has stopped eating or swimming
nodes.why: When a fish with dropsy stops eating or can no longer swim, the illness is usually advanced and often can't be reversed. A vet can tell you whether treatment is still worth trying, or whether euthanasia is kinder.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if the scales start to stand out, or the fish stops eating or swimming normally.
steps: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate, and correct any problem with a partial water change of no more than half the water.
Keep watching the fish: check that its scales stay flat and it keeps eating.
If the scales start to stand out, or it stops eating, start again from the first question.
nodes.title: Possibly pregnant or a full belly
nodes.why: A round belly in a fish that eats and swims normally, with its scales lying flat, may be a pregnancy or a full gut rather than dropsy.

nodes.escalate: Contact an aquatic vet if fish keep dying during or after the full course, or if many fish are breathing fast.
nodes.expert_note: Ichthyophthirius multifiliis. The cycle takes about 3–6 days at 24–26 °C and much longer in cool water, so treatments are spaced by temperature (UF/IFAS: daily in warm water, at least 3–5 treatments). Vets also use salt (about 5 g/L for a week at 24 °C or more), only after checking the species' tolerance with a vet, and salt harms plants; or heat above 30 °C for heat-tolerant species with extra aeration; heat is not reliable on its own. Plants from an infected tank should stand without fish for about a week in a tropical tank, much longer in cool water.
steps: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate first, and fix any problem with a partial water change of no more than half the water.
Choose a white spot treatment and follow the label dose exactly, measured for the real amount of water in the tank, not the tank's sold size.
Remove activated carbon from the filter during treatment, and add an air stone: treatments can lower oxygen.
Keep treating for the full course on the label and past the last spot you can see; in cooler tanks the course takes longer.
Siphon debris from the gravel every other day during treatment, where the parasite's cysts settle.
In future, keep new fish in a separate quarantine tank before adding them to the main tank.
nodes.title: White spot disease (ich)
nodes.why: A common parasite that every freshwater fish can catch. The white spots are the stage feeding under the skin, where medicine can't reach it; the stage that spreads it swims free in the water, and only that stage can be killed. That is why one dose is never enough and treatment continues after the spots go.

nodes.expert_note: Piscinoodinium. Signs: fine yellow to rust-coloured dust or a velvety film, lethargy, poor appetite, flashing, gasping and deaths; no dust shows when only the gills are infected. Diagnosed from skin or gill samples under a microscope. Vets use copper or chloroquine; repeated treatment is needed, and it must run long enough to cover every life stage. Commoner in warm water; affects gouramis and bettas, barbs, danios, killifish and tilapia. The outlook is guarded even with treatment.
steps: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate and correct any problem.
Contact an aquatic vet today and describe the dust; take clear photos.
Ask the vet before using any shop treatment: white spot products may not be the right treatment.
Add an air stone and watch for fast breathing.
When the vet prescribes a treatment, continue it for as long as they advise, so that it covers every stage of the parasite.
nodes.title: Possibly velvet, not white spot
nodes.why: A fine gold or rusty dust is the sign of velvet, a parasite different from white spot. It multiplies fastest in warm water and can overwhelm a tank quickly. It is easily mistaken for white spot, so a vet needs to confirm it, and the treatments vets use for it are not the usual shop products.

nodes.escalate: Ask an aquatic vet before using any medicine. Contact an aquatic vet today if the tufts are on the mouth or gills, the growth spreads within a day, or fish die.
steps: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate; poor water quality often comes first.
Do a partial water change of no more than half the water.
If you can, move the affected fish to a separate tank.
Take clear photos to show a vet.
nodes.title: Cotton-like growths, not white spot
nodes.why: Fluffy tufts are not white spot and need different care. Tufts on a wound or on a fish that is already sick are often a water mould. Tufts on the mouth or lips, or a pale saddle-shaped band, point to a bacterial infection (columnaris), which can spread quickly and needs a vet.

nodes.escalate: If more spots appear on the body or other fish, start again from the first question.
steps: Keep the water clean and test it.
Watch the fish for a few days.
nodes.title: Probably a damaged fin ray, not white spot
nodes.why: A single white spot where a fin is bent or torn is usually a fractured fin ray healing, not a parasite.

nodes.escalate: If the growths spread to the mouth or gills, or the fish stops eating, ask an aquatic vet to confirm.
steps: Keep the water clean and the fish unstressed.
Don't use white spot treatments; they won't help.
nodes.title: Probably lymphocystis, not white spot
nodes.why: Firm, cauliflower-like growths on the fins are usually lymphocystis, a viral infection that is harmless apart from its looks.

options.label: On the newest leaves and shoot tips
The whole plant is turning paler

nodes.text: Where does the damage show first?

steps: Don't add more fertiliser yet: nursery-grown plants carry enough stores for their first 3 to 4 weeks. Plants from laboratory cups are different: they need a little fertiliser within a couple of days.
Remove leaves that melt away.
Change one thing at a time, and judge the result over 2 to 3 weeks on the new leaves.
nodes.title: Probably new leaves replacing old ones
nodes.why: Yellowing on a newly planted plant is often the switch from leaves grown out of water at the nursery to underwater leaves, not a shortage.

nodes.expert_note: Light bands in the app are approximate PAR at the plant: low about 15 to 30, medium 30 to 50, high above about 50 µmol/m²/s (H8-C01). Weak light also shows as long gaps between leaves.
steps: Compare your light with the plant's page: low, medium or high.
Move the plant out of shade, or trim taller plants above it.
Keep the light on 6 to 8 hours a day; more than 10 hours brings algae.
Change one thing at a time, and judge the result over 2 to 3 weeks on the new leaves.
nodes.title: Not enough light
nodes.why: Too little light yellows and weakens plants, and plants shaded by others or by decor suffer first. White LED light, and looking through the water surface, can also make healthy plants look pale.

nodes.expert_note: Without injection a tank sits at about 2 to 3 mg/L CO2 at equilibrium with air, and surface movement drives it out.
steps: If the plant needs CO2 and you don't add it, swap it for an easier plant, or read the CO2 guide before you start.
If you inject CO2 and the drop checker is blue, raise it a little at a time and wait several hours before reading it again; never raise it while it is yellow or fish are gasping.
Change one thing at a time, and judge the result over 2 to 3 weeks on the new leaves.
nodes.title: Not enough CO2
nodes.why: A lack of CO2 also gives yellow leaves and poor growth, and CO2 is the nutrient most likely to limit a planted tank. Rule it out before you change the fertiliser.

nodes.expert_note: Nitrogen, potassium and often magnesium tend to show on older leaves. The pattern comes from land plants and varies between species; no submerged plant has been studied. Pinholes for potassium appear only in aquarium sources, and sources describe phosphorus signs differently (H8-C22). Every aquarium symptom list comes from a seller of fertiliser.
steps: Check your routine against the fertilising guide: liquid fertiliser for plants that feed from the water, root tablets for root feeders.
If you add little or none, start below the dose on the label and raise it slowly while you watch the plants.
Keep testing nitrate: your readings override any dosing.
Change one thing at a time, and judge the result over 2 to 3 weeks on the new leaves.
nodes.title: Older leaves first: a shortage the plant can move
nodes.why: When some nutrients run short, the plant moves them out of its old leaves to feed new growth, so the old leaves yellow, turn see-through or get pinholes first. Leaf colour can't prove which nutrient is short: the signs overlap, and other problems look the same.

nodes.expert_note: Iron and calcium tend to show on new growth: iron as pale new leaves with darker veins, calcium as twisted, stunted new growth, often with magnesium and manganese shortage in very soft water. Too much manganese can cause iron-shortage signs even when iron is present.
steps: Check your routine against the fertilising guide: liquid fertiliser for plants that feed from the water, root tablets for root feeders.
If you add little or none, start below the dose on the label and raise it slowly while you watch the plants.
Keep testing nitrate: your readings override any dosing.
In very soft water, test GH: plants take some minerals from the water itself.
Don't keep adding more of one product to fix it: too much of one nutrient can block another.
Change one thing at a time, and judge the result over 2 to 3 weeks on the new leaves.
nodes.title: New growth first: a shortage the plant can't move
nodes.why: Some nutrients stay where they were laid down, so when they run short the newest leaves come out pale, yellow, twisted or stunted. Leaf colour can't prove which nutrient is short: the signs overlap, and other problems look the same.

steps: Check your routine against the fertilising guide: liquid fertiliser for plants that feed from the water, root tablets for root feeders.
If you add little or none, start below the dose on the label and raise it slowly while you watch the plants.
Keep testing nitrate: your readings override any dosing.
Change one thing at a time, and judge the result over 2 to 3 weeks on the new leaves.
nodes.title: Probably too little fertiliser
nodes.why: Once light and CO2 are ruled out, leaves turning lighter or see-through all over suggest a general lack of fertiliser. Leaf colour can't prove which nutrient is short: the signs overlap, and other problems look the same.

provenance.change_note: New 2026-11-10 from the owner's reviewed h8-deficiency and h8-deficiency-detail chapters (forum demand topic 18), following their proposal: recent planting, light and CO2 first; then where the damage shows; results name a group of causes, never a single nutrient in Guided text (H8-C22 option a); change one thing and wait 2 to 3 weeks; leaf colour is never a diagnosis. Also follows H8-C01, H8-C02 and H8-C07. Expert calls proposed for the owner: 'planted in the last few weeks' as the first split; 'Remove leaves that melt away'; 'judge the result on the new leaves'. Draft until the owner signs it.
